words: rule; fair; safe; reminder
notes: Follow class rules with fewer reminders, and say why a rule exists: to keep people safe, to be fair, to help everyone learn. Rules inside school (line up, take turns) and outside it (crosswalks, the library, a playground sign). The reasoning that grows: a rule has a reason, and a reason can be asked about. Limit: no rule-breaking scenarios that single out a child.

words: job; helper; respect; responsible
notes: Take a class job (line leader, plant waterer, door holder) and a home job, and follow through; name what being helpful and respectful looks like and sounds like. Civic virtue practised in the school setting: doing your part when others count on you. Home jobs are offered as examples only; Teacher note: homes differ, so no child is asked to report on chores done at home.

words: fair; caring; character; in charge
cross_subject: ela:RL.K.3 (characters in a story)
notes: In read-aloud stories and short texts, point to a character who is fair, caring or responsible, a character who is in charge, and a moment where a rule is made or followed. The talk is "How do you know? What did the character do?" so the answer points back to the page. Grade 1 turns this into the qualities of real leaders.

words: listen; take turns; agree; disagree; point of view
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.1 (agreed-upon rules for discussion)
notes: Talk rules for a class circle: listen to the speaker, wait for a turn, answer what was said. Then the first step of perspective: "I like it because ...; my friend likes something else because ...", two points of view about one class question side by side without deciding who is right. Introduces the perspective model at its simplest: different people can see one thing differently, for reasons.

words: I think; because; reason; question
cross_subject: ela:W.K.1 (tell an opinion about a topic)
notes: The spoken "I think ..., because ..." sentence about a class question (Which rule matters most for our class? Which job helps most?), then asking a classmate "Why do you think that?" and answering. Introduces the claim-evidence model: a claim and a reason, with the reason drawn from something the class saw, read or did. D4.1 returns at grade 2 with the reason taken from a source.

words: choose; vote; most; together
cross_subject: math:K.CC.B.5 (count to tell how many voted)
notes: The class makes a real decision together (the name of a class plant, which game at recess): hear the choices, listen to reasons, try for agreement, and when people still differ, vote by a show of hands or by blocks in a tower and count. Then act on the result. The reasoning that grows: a group can decide fairly even when people want different things. Grade 1 names this as voting and elections.

words: flag; stars; stripes; bald eagle; anthem; pledge
cross_subject: ela:RI.K.1 (ask and answer questions about a text)
notes: Use read-alouds to ask and answer questions about the United States flag (13 stripes for the first 13 states, 50 stars for the states now), the bald eagle as the national bird, "The Star-Spangled Banner" as the national anthem and the story of its writing in 1814, and what the words of the Pledge of Allegiance mean in plain words. Teacher note: saying the Pledge is a choice; the Supreme Court ruled in 1943 (West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette) that students cannot be made to say it, and students who stand quietly or do not take part are respected. Each symbol also gets its why-question answered from the record, with what the record says kept apart from what people later said it means: the 1777 flag law set thirteen stripes and thirteen stars but gave no meaning for the colors (the meanings often quoted were written in 1782 for the same colors on the Great Seal and only later applied to the flag); the bald eagle was picked for the Great Seal in 1782 as a bird found only in North America; and Congress made "The Star-Spangled Banner" the national anthem by law in 1931. Students sort each statement into "the record says" or "people say it means".

words: near; far; left; right; behind; between; next to
cross_subject: math:K.G.A.1 (position words for objects)
notes: Say where people, objects and places are with position words: near, far, left, right, behind, in front of, between, next to. Practised in the room, on the playground and on simple picture maps of the classroom. This is the language every later map skill uses.

words: map; globe; land; water; Earth
notes: A globe is a model of the whole round Earth; a map is a flat drawing of a place, as if seen from above. Compare them: both show land and water, a globe is round and shows the whole Earth, a map can be folded and can show a small place. Find land and water on each.

words: address; street; town; city; state; country
notes: The parts of an address: number and street, city or town, state, country (the United States). With help, find the school's town on a map of the student's own state, and the school on a street map of the town. Curio Class teaches the student's own state where the anchor names Massachusetts, worked through with two or three example states. Teacher note: some children do not have a stable home address; practise with the school's address, never require a child's own.

words: map; symbol; key; hill; pond; path
notes: Use photographs, drawings and simple maps to show where places near the school are (the playground, the library, a park) and how they relate (the park is next to the library). Make maps, drawings and block models of familiar places, showing physical features such as a hill, a pond or trees. Introduces the map-key model: a small picture stands for a real thing, and a box on the side says what each picture means.

words: holiday; honor; remember; history
notes: Civic holidays remember a person or an event: Independence Day (the Declaration, 1776), Martin Luther King Jr. Day (his work against unfair laws), Presidents' Day, Veterans Day, Memorial Day, and Indigenous Peoples' Day or Columbus Day as communities observe them. For each: who or what is remembered, and why. Teacher note: Thanksgiving is taught from the record at this age (the 1621 harvest meal shared by Wampanoag people and English settlers) and from what Wampanoag people say about it today; the Wampanoag nations live in Massachusetts now. No headdress or costume play of Native people.

words: tradition; celebrate; culture; same; different
notes: Compare and contrast how people from different cultural backgrounds celebrate and keep traditions (foods, songs, special days, ways of greeting), through books and invited family guests: what is alike, what is different. Uses the perspective model: people do things differently for reasons that matter to them. Teacher note: religious traditions are described, never practised in class; no child is asked to share a tradition, and families who do not celebrate a holiday are respected.

words: first; next; last; before; after; yesterday; today; tomorrow; long ago
cross_subject: ela:RI.K.3 (connect events in a text)
notes: Put events in order from the child's own day, from nature (a seed grows into a plant) and from a story, using sequence words (first, next, last) and time words (now, then, long ago, before, after, yesterday, today, tomorrow). Introduces the timeline model as a picture strip read left to right. D2.His.1 is met here with three or four events in order; grade 1 adds the calendar and dated events.

words: long ago; today; old; new; photograph; object
notes: Compare life long ago with life today through old photographs and objects (a washboard and a washing machine, a slate and a tablet, a horse cart and a bus): what changed, what stayed the same (people still wash clothes, go to school, travel). Old photos and objects are clues that help us learn about the past. Introduces the continuity-change model as a two-column chart, then and now.

words: work; job; worker; skill; tool
notes: With help, describe work people do inside and outside the home (caring for children, cooking, building, nursing, farming, driving a bus), using experience and books, and the skills and tools each job needs. Work at home counts as work even when it is not paid.

words: need; want; buy; sell; trade; choose
notes: With help, ask and answer questions about buying, selling and trading (a class store with play money, a trade of one sticker for another), tell needs (food, water, shelter, clothing) from wants, and explain that people cannot have everything, so they choose. The reasoning that grows: choosing because there is not enough of everything (scarcity). Teacher note: keep examples away from what a child's family can or cannot afford.

words: goods; services; money; earn; pay
notes: With help, give examples of goods (things you can hold: apples, shoes) and services (things people do for you: a haircut, a bus ride, a doctor's visit) that people pay for with money they earn by working.

words: question; wonder; why; how
cross_subject: ela:SL.K.3 (ask and answer questions to learn more)
notes: Ask "I wonder" questions about the class's topic (Why do we have rules? Why is the flag red, white and blue?) and say why a question matters to us. The class keeps a wonder wall and returns to it at the end of a unit to see which questions were answered.

words: group; member; belong; duty; rule
notes: What belonging to a group means (a family, a class, a team, a club) and what it gives (help, friendship, shared work); following a group's rules and duties, and giving the reason for each rule. Builds on kindergarten's "a rule has a reason" by asking how a group's rules serve its purpose.

words: role; goal; share; community; teamwork
notes: Investigate the roles in a group with a shared goal (a class garden, a school play, a community clean-up) and explain how each role helps reach it; how a community gets common work done, from firefighters to volunteers. Every member matters, not only the person in charge.

words: leader; responsibility; organize; guide; quality
cross_subject: ela:RI.1.3 (connect two individuals or ideas in a text)
notes: A leader is a group member who takes on extra responsibility: inspiring others, organizing tasks, guiding decisions. Study leaders from history, daily life and texts (a principal, a crossing guard, Harriet Tubman, Abraham Lincoln, Wilma Mankiller, the first woman to be Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, Cesar Chavez) and ask questions about how each person made a change. Name the qualities of a good leader with evidence from what the leader did. Leaders are chosen from many backgrounds, women and men.

words: vote; election; fair; majority; ballot
cross_subject: math:1.MD.C.4 (organize and compare tallied data)
notes: Groups whose members want different things need a fair way to decide; voting is one way, and an election is voting to choose a leader. Hold a class election with secret ballots, tally the votes and read the result. The democratic ideas behind it: each vote counts the same (equality), the rules are the same for everyone (fairness), and people accept a fair result.

words: President; governor; mayor; government; citizen; term
notes: Some leaders are chosen by election: the President, the student's own state governor (the anchor names Massachusetts), a mayor, a team captain; what each does. Government is the group that makes and carries out a community's rules and provides services everyone uses (schools, roads, parks, fire stations). Citizens elect leaders for a set number of years and judge whether to elect them again. Native nations are governments too: many elect their own leaders today, such as a tribal chair or chief.

words: citizen; community member; rights; responsibilities; improve
notes: People born in the United States are citizens; others become citizens later; some people who live here are not citizens and are still members of the community with rights and responsibilities. What makes a good citizen or community member, from history, texts, news and the child's own life, including people who worked to make their communities better over time (a library founder, a neighborhood clean-up). Teacher note: never ask about any child's or family's citizenship or immigration status; every child has the right to a public education (Plyler v. Doe, Supreme Court, 1982).

words: map; space; location; symbol; key; globe
notes: A map stands for real space, seen from above and made smaller, and helps people find places and features. Read the key of simple maps (a school map, a park map, a town map) and use maps and globes to find what places are like: land or water, town or farmland. The map-key model now names its symbols for real places.

words: north; south; east; west; capital; city
notes: Use the cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) to find and describe places on a map; find major cities and capitals and ask why each became important (a harbor, a river crossing, a seat of government). A capital is the city where a state or nation's government meets: Washington, D.C., and the student's own state capital. Introduces the compass-directions model.

words: continent; ocean; river; lake; mountain; landform
cross_subject: science:K-ESS3-1 (people live where their needs are met)
notes: Find continents, oceans, rivers, lakes and mountains on maps and the globe, with names for the biggest (the seven continents and five oceans, met here and learned to place in grade 2), and make a map of a local place with its water and land. The physical features named here are the vocabulary of grade 2's world geography.

words: custom; language; way of life; culture
notes: People in different parts of the world can have different ways of living, customs and languages: compare homes, foods, clothing for the weather, school days and greetings in three or four places, with present-day photographs, not only traditional dress. Uses perspective: a way of life makes sense to the people who live it. Limit: no "exotic" framing; people today live in cities and towns everywhere.

words: united; diverse; history; belief; tradition
notes: Use evidence to explain how people in the United States are united (a shared national history, the same Constitution and laws, shared holidays) and how they are diverse (backgrounds, beliefs, languages, traditions, including the Native nations who were here first and live here now). Students give a claim with a piece of evidence from a text or photograph. The reasoning that grows: one country can hold many different people.

words: symbol; motto; White House; Statue of Liberty; E pluribus unum
notes: Grows kindergarten's symbols: the White House, the Statue of Liberty (a gift from France, raised in 1886, read by many newcomers as a sign of welcome), the motto "E pluribus unum" (Out of many, one) and what the words of the Pledge mean; recognize the tunes and words of "America the Beautiful" and "The Star-Spangled Banner". Teacher note: singing and the Pledge are a choice for every student (West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, 1943).

words: calendar; month; year; past; present; future; season
cross_subject: science:1-ESS1-2 (patterns of daylight across the seasons)
notes: Record seasonal events and personal experiences on a calendar (birthdays, the first snow, the last day of school) and talk about them with past, present and future verb forms (yesterday we went, today we go, tomorrow we will go). Depth: D2.His.1 deepens from kindergarten: events now carry a date, and a year is read as one long row of months on the timeline model.

words: source; photograph; letter; artifact; interview
cross_subject: ela:RI.1.6 (information from pictures and from words)
notes: Name the kinds of sources about the past (photographs, letters, objects, maps, buildings, stories people tell) and, for a class question, pick which kinds would help answer it. Used on then-and-now comparisons of the school or town, so continuity-change grows from objects to a whole place.

words: employed; income; wages; salary; earn
notes: Being employed means working for pay; income is the money a person earns; wages are pay by the hour, a salary is pay by the year. People earn income by working, and some earn it by selling what they make or grow. Grade 1 owns this standard for the band (the anchor shares it with grade 2).

words: goods; services; price; market; buyer; seller
notes: Give examples of goods people buy and use and services people do for each other, sort them, and find prices of a few things at a local market or store flyer. Grows kindergarten's goods and services into buying in a real market. Grade 1 owns these standards for the band.

words: choice; limited; give up; cost; benefit
notes: Limited money means choosing: food for the family or a toy, bus fare to work or a movie ticket. Name the benefit and the cost of a choice, and what is given up (introduces the opportunity-cost model as "the next best thing you did not choose"). Some choices are about values: buying from a business that treats its workers well or cares for the land. Teacher note: examples stay general, never about a classmate's family.

words: save; spend; share; donate; emergency; bank
cross_subject: math:1.OA.A.1 (add and subtract within 20)
notes: Compare reasons to save: for a later purchase, to give to a cause, for an emergency. A bank keeps money safe and pays a little for keeping it. Introduces the budget model as three jars (spend, save, share) and a small amount split among them. Saving now means giving up something now, the opportunity-cost model again.

words: big question; small question; history; geography; economics; government
notes: A big (compelling) question is broken into smaller (supporting) questions, each of which helps answer it: for "What makes a good leader?", "What did this leader do?" and "How did people feel about it?". Name which part of social studies a question belongs to (history, geography, civics, economics). For each supporting question the class lists the facts and the ideas needed to answer it (for "What did this leader do?": the leader's actions and the words leader and change), so every small question is tied to what must be learned to answer it.

words: explain; first; then; because; reason
cross_subject: ela:W.1.1 (opinion with a reason and a closing)
notes: Write and say short explanations in the right order with the facts that matter ("First the class voted, then we counted, so the plant is called Leafy"), and ask and answer questions about a classmate's explanation. The claim-evidence model now in writing: a claim, a reason, a closing.

words: problem; solution; community; help; action
notes: Name a problem in the school or local community (litter on the playground, a crosswalk that feels unsafe), find out how people are already working on it, and list ways the class could help. Hearing more than one view first uses the perspective model. Action is the students' choice informed by what they found, never a cause picked for them. Then one step wider: from a picture book or photo set, the class sees the same kind of problem (litter, unsafe streets, clean water) in other towns, in the region and in another country, and names one way people there work on it. This is grade 1's yearly action cycle: the class chooses one way to help with its own problem, decides it by the secret-ballot class election (ss1-voting), carries it out through the school, and looks back at what changed.

words: title; key; compass rose; scale; environment
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure length with a ruler)
notes: What each part of a map tells us: the title (what the map shows), the key (what symbols mean), the compass rose (directions) and the scale (how far a length on the map is on the ground). Introduces the map-scale model with whole units ("this line is one block"). Examples of maps that show how people live with the land: a farm map, a city park map, a flood map.

words: projection; flat; round; size; shape
notes: A round Earth cannot be drawn flat without stretching something. Compare a Mercator map (shapes kept, lands far from the equator drawn too big: Greenland looks as large as Africa) with a Peters map (sizes kept, shapes stretched) and the globe, which is right about both. The reasoning that grows: every map makes choices, so ask what a map shows well and what it bends.

words: map; title; key; scale; neighborhood
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measure length with a ruler)
notes: Make a map of a familiar place (the school, a neighborhood block, a park) with a title, a key, a compass rose and a simple scale. Depth: D2.Geo.1 deepens from kindergarten: the kindergarten picture map becomes a map with all four parts, and distances are shown in repeated whole units (each step of the scale bar is one block or ten paces), counted, not yet measured with a ruler.

words: continent; ocean; mountain range; river; desert; equator
cross_subject: science:2-ESS2-2 (model shapes and kinds of land and water)
notes: Locate the seven continents and the five oceans on a world map and a globe, and some major features on each continent (the Andes, the Amazon, the Sahara, the Nile, the Himalayas, the Great Lakes, the Rocky Mountains). Why oceans matter: food, trade routes, weather, most of the planet's water and life. Describe where each continent lies with the compass directions.

words: climate; weather; region; rainforest; desert; mountain
cross_subject: science:K-ESS2-1 (weather patterns over time)
notes: Where land and water lie shapes weather, climate and what grows there: near the equator it is warm all year, high mountains are cold, land by the sea has milder winters, deserts get little rain. Weather is today, climate is the pattern over many years. Introduces the region model: an area that shares something (a desert region, a rainforest region), and how life there fits it. Then one region at two dates: two photographs or maps of the same place years apart (a glacier that shrank, a lake that dried, a forest that grew back) to say what changed in its environment and give one reason why.

words: environment; adapt; change; disaster; need
cross_subject: science:K-ESS3-3 (ways to reduce human impact on land and water)
notes: How people use and change their environment (farming terraces, dams, cities by rivers) and how they adapt to it (houses on stilts, warm clothing); how people in a city, a town and a farm community meet daily needs from nearby and far away; how a flood, an earthquake or a hurricane can affect people living in a place and how they help each other recover. Teacher note: a child may have lived through a disaster; examples are told calmly and end with how people helped. Grade 2's yearly action cycle: after learning how people in a place get ready for and recover from a storm or flood, the class chooses one way to help its own school community get ready (a class-made poster or a short announcement to another class on what to do in a storm), checks it against the town's or state's published advice, decides by a fair vote, carries it out through the school, and talks about what happened. Action is the class's choice informed by what it learned, never a cause picked for it.

words: migrate; move; chosen; forced; refugee; reason
notes: Why people move to new places: work, family, safety, land, freedom. Some moves are chosen; some are forced. Forced moves named plainly at grade level: Africans captured and brought to the Americas in chains and enslaved; Native nations such as the Cherokee forced from their homelands by the United States government in the 1830s; refugees fleeing war today. Students list possible reasons for a move and pick which reasons best explain it. Introduces the cause-effect-chain model (a reason, the move, what happened next). Native nations appear in the present tense too: the Cherokee Nation governs itself today in Oklahoma, and the Eastern Band of Cherokee still lives in its North Carolina homeland. Teacher note: plain facts, the human side, no role play or simulation of capture, removal or flight.

words: immigrant; newcomer; ancestor; nation; welcome
notes: Why the United States is called "a nation of immigrants": many families came from every continent, by choice, at many times, and still do. Then the honest limits of the phrase, answered from facts: Native nations were here first and are not immigrants; Africans who were enslaved did not choose to come. Compare what newcomers long ago (letters and memories from Ellis Island and Angel Island) and newcomers today say about arriving. Teacher note: some children are immigrants or refugees themselves; no child is asked to tell a family story.

words: interview; question; family; memory; generation
cross_subject: ela:SL.2.3 (ask and answer questions about what a speaker says)
notes: Write questions, then interview a family member, neighbor or school staff member about where their family came from, how and why they moved, and when they came to this town or state (the anchor names Massachusetts). An interview is a historical source: ask what it can and cannot tell us. Put the answers on a timeline. Teacher note: families differ (adoption, foster care, a refugee story, an unknown past); a student may interview any trusted adult, and no one is asked about immigration status.

words: culture; language; food; music; belief; enrich
notes: What makes up a culture (language, food, music, beliefs, holidays, art, ways of dress), what people bring when they move, and how migration changes both the newcomers and the place they come to (foods, words and music now shared by everyone). How all of a community's people, newcomers and long-time residents and Native nations, make it richer. Uses the cause-effect-chain: a move, then what changed.

words: source; maker; date; place; fact; opinion
cross_subject: ela:RI.2.6 (the main purpose of a text)
notes: Before using a source, find from the source itself who made it, when and where (a dated photo, a signed letter, a labeled map). Tell a fact (can be checked) from an opinion (what someone thinks). Introduces the source-sourcing model as three questions on a card: who made it, when, where.

words: account; same; different; agree; compare; copy
cross_subject: ela:RI.2.9 (compare two texts on the same topic)
notes: Compare two accounts of the same event (two newcomers' memories of one ship arrival, two newspaper reports of a town flood): what both say, where they differ, and why two people might tell it differently. Introduces the corroboration model at its simplest: when two sources agree, we can trust that part more, but only after checking that each teller had their own way of knowing (two people who both saw the flood, not one newspaper repeating another), since two copies of one account are really one account.

words: country; border; continent; government; flag; capital
notes: Physical geography (land and water, such as Africa as one continent) is different from political geography (countries and their borders: Africa holds more than 50 independent countries). What makes a country: land with borders, people, a government, laws, and usually a capital and a flag. Read physical and political maps of the same continent side by side.

words: research; report; source; fact; present
cross_subject: ela:W.2.7 (shared research and writing projects)
notes: Choose a country outside the United States (where a family came from, a place in a favorite story, a country with an animal or landscape of interest), gather facts from one or two sources picked for what they are and how they are built, and present a short report on its land, resources and people today, with a map. Each supporting question links to the big one. Limit: people shown in the present day, in cities and towns as well as the countryside; no stereotypes. The report ends with an argument, not only a list of facts: one claim about the country that answers the big question ("Its rivers matter most to how people live there") with two facts from the sources that back it.

words: claim; evidence; source; reason
cross_subject: ela:W.2.1 (opinion with reasons and linking words)
notes: Write a claim with reasons taken from a named source ("Oceans matter because ... The map shows ..."). Depth: D4.1 deepens from kindergarten: the spoken "I think, because" now names where the reason came from. The claim-evidence model carries a source.

words: natural resource; renewable; non-renewable; industry; produce
cross_subject: science:K-ESS3-1 (people use what the land provides)
notes: How a place's natural resources connect to its industries and jobs (fishing on a coast, farming on plains, mining in mountains, lumber in forests), with places in the student's region and in the countries studied; renewable resources (trees, water, wind) and non-renewable ones (oil, coal, metals); goods made in our community and goods made in other places; what it costs to make a good (materials, tools, workers). Grade 2 owns the resources part of the shared economics topic.

words: skill; knowledge; invention; tool; human resource
notes: People are a resource too: what they learn at school and at work leads to new inventions and more goods and services. Tools and machines that make goods (a tractor, a sewing machine) and the skills of the people who use them.

words: trade; import; export; goods; far away
notes: Why people in one country trade with people in other countries (each has resources and skills the other lacks); find things at home made abroad (bananas, a T-shirt, a phone) and things made here and sold abroad, and trace them on a world map. What we buy connects us to people in distant places. A choice to buy one thing still means giving up another (opportunity-cost).

words: map; title; legend; scale; landmark; cardinal direction
cross_subject: math:2.MD.A.1 (measuring a length with a ruler)
notes: Unit 1. Read a current map of the student's own town with title, legend, directions and scale, and find its physical features and landmarks; then draw a simple map of the school grounds or neighborhood with all four parts. Scale, met in grade 2 as repeated whole units, is used to count rough distances in whole bar lengths (the library is about three bars from school); grade 4 measures with a ruler, uses parts of a bar and converts to miles or kilometres. Massachusetts's own-town map standard taught in general form: every class maps its own town, with worked examples from towns in several states. D2.Geo.1 here builds a map of a familiar place; grade 4 builds maps of a whole state.

words: globe; continent; ocean; equator; prime meridian; hemisphere; grid
cross_subject: science:3-ESS2-2 (climates differ among regions of the world)
notes: Unit 1. The globe as a model of Earth and a flat map as a picture of it; the seven continents and five oceans (a review of grade 2's world year); the equator and the prime meridian as the two zero lines that split Earth into hemispheres; a letter-and-number grid to find a place on a map. Why places near the equator are warm and places near the poles are cold, and why that matters for how people live. Latitude and longitude are named as lines here and used with numbers in grade 4. Warmth is not the only cause: places at a similar distance from the equator can still differ because of rain (a desert and a wet forest at about the same latitude), so students name two reasons world regions differ.

words: region; state; capital; river; lake; coast; mountain range
cross_subject: science:2-ESS2-2 (modelling the land and water of an area)
notes: Unit 1. Find the student's own state among the fifty on a political map and the US region it belongs to; on a physical map of the region, name its main rivers, lakes, coast and mountains, and say how they shape where towns are (towns at rivers, harbors and passes). Region (grade 2's climate regions) now names a group of US states that share features. Massachusetts's New England standards taught in general form: own state and own region, with worked examples rotated across regions.

words: environment; adapt; modify; dam; farmland; change over time
cross_subject: science:K-ESS3-3 (people change the land and can reduce their impact)
notes: Unit 1. How people have changed the land around them (fields, dams, roads, filled wetlands, parks) and how their ways of life shaped those changes; an early map of the student's own place set beside a modern one to find what changed and what stayed. Native nations shaped the land too (burning, farming, trails) and are named as present in the place today.

words: government; local; state; national; mayor; council; governor; president; tax; service
notes: Unit 2. Why schools, towns, states and the country have governments and what each does; the three levels and who leads each (mayor or town manager and council or town meeting; governor and legislature; president and Congress); how city and town governments differ in form; how taxes and fees pay for services such as schools, roads, fire and water. Taught for the student's own town and state, with worked examples from several states. Tribal nations are named as governments too, with their own leaders and laws. Builds on ss1-elected-leaders (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's grade 2 civics is countries and their governments only; this civic skill was last taught at grade 1. Depth: D2.Civ.1 here names the levels and what each does; grade 5 (ss5-constitution) completes it with what each branch is responsible for at the national level. Handoff kind: from ss1-elected-leaders (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-elected-leaders.

words: rule; law; right; responsibility; freedom; fair
notes: Unit 2. Why groups make rules and laws: to keep people safe, settle disputes and protect freedoms; every right comes with responsibilities (the right to speak and the duty to let others speak). Students trace one school rule and one town law back to the problem it solves. Depth: D2.Civ.3 here asks what a rule is for; grade 5 (ss5-constitution) reads real constitutional provisions and asks why each was written. Builds on ss1-citizens (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's grade 2 civics is countries and their governments only; this civic skill was last taught at grade 1. Handoff kind: from ss1-citizens (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-citizens.

words: citizen; vote; volunteer; election; meeting; participate
notes: Unit 2. How a democracy depends on people taking part: voting, public meetings, serving on boards, volunteering, staying informed; what people gain and what is hard about working together in families, schools, workplaces and government. Compare how a decision is made in the classroom, at a town meeting or council, and in an election. Builds on ss1-voting (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's grade 2 civics is countries and their governments only; this civic skill was last taught at grade 1. Handoff kind: from ss1-voting (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-voting.

words: discuss; agree; disagree; point of view; majority; compromise
cross_subject: ela:SL.3.1 (collaborative discussion rules)
notes: Unit 2. Disagreeing respectfully: listen, restate another's view, give a reason for one's own, and notice the experiences and values behind different points of view on a real class question. Ends in a class vote after a structured discussion, with the minority's view heard first. The question is a real class choice the class can act on, never a contested public issue picked by the course. Builds on ss1-community-problems (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's grade 2 civics is countries and their governments only; this civic skill was last taught at grade 1. Handoff kind: from ss1-community-problems (grade 1) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by ss2-people-environment.

words: constitution; state constitution; legislature; plan of government
notes: Unit 2. Every state has its own constitution that sets up its government and lists its people's rights; students find two or three things in their own state's constitution from the state's official pages. Massachusetts's 1780 constitution, mainly written by John Adams and the oldest written constitution still in use, is one worked example among several states, not the subject. Then a comparison: where the state constitution sets up the same three parts as the US Constitution, where it differs (how judges are chosen, ballot questions), and one other system (a tribal nation's published constitution or another country's), saying where each came from and what each part does.

words: Declaration of Independence; independence; Constitution; Bill of Rights; consent; symbol; holiday
notes: Unit 6. Why colonists felt treated unfairly and declared independence (in brief); what the Declaration says about rights and government by consent of the governed; what a constitution is for and that the Bill of Rights lists rights; that full citizenship in the new country was limited to white men who owned property, and who was left out (women, enslaved people, Native nations, poor men). National symbols, songs and patriotic holidays and the ideas they stand for. The Revolution's events are left to grade 5 (ss5-revolution-causes, ss5-independence-war), which assume this row across grade 4 because grade 4 teaches no founding content. Builds on ss1-national-symbols (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because national symbols are a kindergarten and grade 1 topic in Massachusetts; grade 2 has none. Handoff kind: from ss1-national-symbols (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-national-symbols.

words: goods; services; producer; consumer; natural resource; human resource; capital resource; profit
notes: Unit 3. What the community makes and does to earn a living: goods and services, producers and consumers, the natural, human and capital resources a business uses (a bakery's flour, bakers and ovens), and how hoping for profit leads sellers to choose what to sell and at what price. Taught from local businesses, with worked examples from several communities.

words: scarcity; choice; cost; benefit; opportunity cost; incentive
notes: Unit 3. Scarcity: people and communities cannot have everything they want, so they choose. Compare the costs and benefits of a choice and name what is given up (opportunity cost); notice rewards and penalties (incentives) that push choices, such as a sale price or a late fee. Builds on grade 1's choices: opportunity cost is now named as the next-best thing given up. Builds on ss1-choices (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's shared grade 1 and 2 economics topic is taught once, at grade 1 (see social-studies-excluded.csv), so grade 2 does not carry it. Handoff kind: from ss1-choices (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-choices.

words: barter; money; save; spend; bank; interest; budget; goal; credit union; insurance; interest rate
cross_subject: math:2.MD.C.8 (money problems in dollars and cents); math:3.NBT.A.2 (adding and subtracting within 1000)
notes: Unit 3. Why money makes trading easier than barter; a bank keeps money safe and pays interest on savings and charges it on loans; a simple savings plan toward a goal, tracking money in and money out over several weeks. Builds on grade 1's saving. All amounts are made-up class examples; no student shares family money facts. Builds on ss1-saving (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's shared grade 1 and 2 economics topic is taught once, at grade 1 (see social-studies-excluded.csv), so grade 2 does not carry it. Banks are not the only places that keep or lend money: a credit union is a bank-like place owned by its members, and an insurance company collects small regular payments from many people so it can pay for one person's big loss. Interest is the price of using money: a bank pays savers a little and charges borrowers more, which is how it earns; when the rate goes up, savers earn more and borrowers pay more. Handoff kind: from ss1-saving (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-saving.

words: import; export; trade; depend; world
notes: Unit 3. What is made in the community and what comes from far away (read from labels and a world map); trading makes places depend on each other. One comparison with how people earn and spend in a community in another country, chosen so the elementary course does not repeat the same country. Depth: D2.Eco.14 here notices that goods travel between countries; grade 4 (ss4-trade-north-america) explains why nations trade and who gains.

words: timeline; year; decade; century; past; present; era
cross_subject: math:2.MD.B.6 (equally spaced points on a number line)
notes: Thread through every history unit. Read and build timelines in years, decades and centuries, with equal spaces for equal spans of time; place events from first meetings, the early colonies and the founding, and from the community's own history, on one class timeline; say which came first and how far apart. Depth: D2.His.1 here orders events on one line; grade 4 (ss4-exploration) draws a timeline to scale and compares things happening at the same time in different places.

words: source; primary source; secondary source; artifact; author; date; first-hand
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.7 (information from maps, photographs and illustrations)
notes: Thread through the year. Tell a primary source from a secondary one by how it relates to the question: a primary source is first-hand evidence for what is being studied (an object, a record, a photograph, or the words of someone who was there, even when those words were written down or recorded years later, like a memoir or the grade 2 family interviews), and a secondary source explains or interprets the past from other sources (a textbook page, a museum label). Date alone does not decide it: students ask how the source relates to the question, then when it was made, why, and what it cannot show. The grade 2 interview is one of the worked examples; ask who made it and when before using it; ask questions about two or three sources on one event. Builds on grade 2's who made a source; grade 4 adds for whom and why.

words: Native nation; tribe; homeland; sovereignty; reservation; contribution; tradition
notes: Unit 4. The Native nation or nations of the student's own region, past and present: their names for themselves, homelands, how rivers, coasts and land shaped where towns and seasonal camps were, foods, crafts, words, place names and knowledge they gave the wider country, and that these nations govern themselves today with their own governments, lands and laws. Taught from each nation's own published materials, with worked examples from five regions settled in the course frame. Present tense as well as past. Massachusetts's regional standard taught in general form (own region). Teacher note: sacred or restricted knowledge is not taught; no costumes, headdresses or crafts that copy sacred objects; the class finds whose land the school is on from the nations' own pages. Sovereignty is defined as a nation's right to govern itself; the class uses that phrase until the word is secure.

words: explorer; voyage; Atlantic; route; encounter; describe
notes: Unit 5. Find North America, the Atlantic and Europe; why Europeans sailed west in the 1500s and 1600s (trade, riches, land, religion) as causes leading to effects; the routes of explorers along more than one coast (for example Cabot, Verrazzano, Champlain, John Smith, and Spanish voyages to Florida) traced on a map; how one explorer described the Native people and land he met, read beside what that nation says of itself; an early 1600s map compared with a modern one. Massachusetts's Northeast standards taught in general form across several coasts.

words: colony; colonist; settlement; self-government; compact; leader; conflict
notes: Unit 5. Two or three early colonies and their Native neighbors, for example Plymouth and the Wampanoag, Jamestown and the Powhatan, St. Augustine and the Timucua: who came and why, how they governed themselves (the Mayflower Compact as the short case of self-government), the hardships families faced, and how Native leaders (Massasoit, Wahunsenaca, Metacom) and colonial leaders (Bradford, Winthrop) chose differently. As colonies spread, Native nations lost land, many died of new diseases, and wars followed, including King Philip's War; told from both sides as two perspectives. The harvest-feast story taught from the record (the few lines written at the time) and from what Wampanoag people say about it today; the Wampanoag nations live and govern today. Teacher note: disease, war and land loss named plainly; no reenactment of the feast or of conflict.

words: artifact; daily life; chore; apprentice; servant; then and now
notes: Unit 5. Use paintings, tools, houses and short texts to describe daily life, homes, schooling and work in an early colony, including servants and enslaved people, and compare it with life today: what changed and what stayed the same.

words: slavery; enslaved; free; legal; cruel; resist
notes: Unit 5. Slavery was legal in every European colony in the 1600s and 1700s, north and south; African people and some Native people were enslaved, and some Africans in the colonies were free. Taught plainly at grade level: who was enslaved, that it was legal and cruel, and that enslaved people resisted and built families and lives. Teacher note: people are named as enslaved people, not slaves as an identity; no role play or simulation; enslaved people's own words where they exist.

words: port; harbor; fishing; shipbuilding; trade route; Triangular Trade
notes: Unit 5. How trade by sea and bartering built colonial economies: fishing and shipbuilding, port towns that grew around harbors, and the trade routes that carried goods and people across the Atlantic and to the Caribbean, including the Triangular Trade that sold enslaved Africans and moved goods made by their forced labor. Taught through ports in more than one colony, not one state's seaports. Depth: D2.Geo.7 here follows goods and people on one set of routes; grade 4 (ss4-regional-cultures) compares how people moved into each US region over two centuries. Teacher note: the trade in people named plainly as part of the economy, not a side note.

words: community; founder; immigrant; newcomer; interview; population; celebration
cross_subject: ela:W.3.7 (short research project); ela:SL.3.4 (reporting on a topic)
notes: Unit 7. The local history project: who has lived in the community over time (the Native nation or nations, founders, enslaved and free workers, immigrants and newcomers today), why people move, and local celebrations and traditions, from interviews with family and neighbors, old photographs and a historical map of the student's own state; what changed and what stayed. Findings are shared with someone outside the class (a library display, a town office, families). Massachusetts's own-town standards taught in general form. Teacher note: no student is asked to share family immigration or legal status; interview questions are chosen by the family.

words: biography; achievement; contribution; leader; change
cross_subject: ela:W.3.2 (informative writing); ela:W.3.7 (short research project)
notes: Thread, ending in unit 7. Ask questions about people who made a difference, local and national, men and women of many backgrounds; each student writes one short biography of a person who shaped the community, in time order with details from at least two sources. Builds on ss1-leaders (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because grade 2 has no biography or leaders topic; grade 1 last taught how a person made a change. Handoff kind: from ss1-leaders (grade 1) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss1-leaders.

words: question; compelling question; supporting question; inquiry; answer
notes: Every unit. The inquiry arc at its first full turn: a compelling question no lookup settles, set by the teacher; why it matters to others; supporting questions written together as a class, each answered on a day; how the supporting answers build the bigger one. Depth: grade 3 writes supporting questions together from a given compelling question; grade 5 (ss5-civil-rights-research) writes its own supporting questions for a chosen topic. With each compelling question the class names one idea people could understand differently (what "fair" or "a good leader" means) and hears two ways of seeing it; with each supporting question it lists the facts and ideas needed to answer it.

words: claim; evidence; reason; because; source
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (opinion writing with reasons)
notes: Every unit. Grow a spoken "I think, because" into a short written claim that answers the unit question, with one or two pieces of evidence, each from a named source, and a reason that links them. Depth: grade 3 uses evidence given in the unit's sources; grade 5 (ss5-civil-rights-research) gathers evidence from several sources it finds.

words: community; problem; action; plan; decide; contribute
notes: Unit 7, once in the year. The class names a local problem from its project, weighs two or three ways to help and what each might do, decides by a fair process, and makes one contribution to the community. Action is the class's evidence-based choice, never a cause the course picks. Depth: grade 3 acts as a class with the teacher guiding each step; grade 5 (ss5-informed-action) plans in small groups and predicts results. Builds on ss1-community-problems (grade 1); the handoff skips a grade because Massachusetts's grade 2 civics is countries and their governments only; this civic skill was last taught at grade 1. Handoff kind: from ss1-community-problems (grade 1) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by ss2-people-environment.

words: scale; key; compass rose; physical feature
cross_subject: math:4.MD.A.2 (distance problems)
notes: Find distances between places with a map's scale bar; read a key, title and directions; locate the physical features of North America. Grade 2 showed scale in repeated whole units and grade 3 counted whole bar lengths; here students measure with a ruler, use parts of a bar and convert to miles or kilometres. Students also compare the same place on maps of different scales (a town map, a state map, a map of North America) and say what each scale shows and what it hides (D2.Geo.3).

words: continent; country; state; province; territory; county; latitude; longitude
notes: Locate Canada and its provinces and territories, Mexico and its states, the Caribbean nations and the United States on a political map, and use the words continent, country, state, province and county correctly. Find a place by its latitude and longitude in whole degrees, building on grade 3's equator, prime meridian and grid.

words: research; atlas; credible; fact; opinion; present
cross_subject: ela:W.4.7 (short research project); ela:SL.4.4 (reporting on a topic)
notes: Research Canada or Mexico (its people and languages, government, cities, land and industries) from maps, atlases, articles and digital sources; choose sources that fit the question, sort fact from opinion to judge which sources to trust, and present findings; classmates critique each explanation for order, detail and accuracy. Indigenous peoples of each country (First Nations, Inuit and Métis in Canada; Indigenous peoples of Mexico) are named in the present. Depth: D1.5 here picks kinds of sources for a given topic; grade 5 picks sources for a question students wrote. Source choice uses two named tests: does the set hold more than one view on the question (for a shared issue such as trade across the border, a Canadian or Mexican source beside a US one), and what does each source's origin, kind and date say about using it. Students check one fact in two sources and note where they agree.

words: archaeologist; artifact; evidence; theory; migration
cross_subject: science:4-ESS1-1 (rock layers as evidence of change over time)
notes: How people first reached North America: competing theories (a land bridge, a coastal sea route) weighed against dated evidence of people here about 15,000 years ago or earlier; what digs, artifacts and climate data can and cannot show; Native culture regions on a map. Native nations' own accounts of their origins are named as their own, beside the archaeology, not ranked against it.

words: descendant; nation; preserve; sacred
notes: Mesa Verde, Cahokia and other preserved places, and the nations who count their builders as ancestors and live and govern today (the Pueblo nations of the Southwest; several nations, such as the Osage, for Cahokia). Past and present tense together, from the nations' own published materials; sacred or restricted knowledge left out. Teacher note: these are ancestral places of living nations, not ruins of vanished peoples.

words: primary source; secondary source; purpose; audience; corroborate
cross_subject: ela:RI.4.6 (firsthand and secondhand accounts)
notes: Tell a primary source from a secondary one, and before using a source ask who made it, when, for whom and why. Sources of the voyage era: maps, drawings, journals and objects. Depth: D2.His.11 here infers audience and purpose from clues in one source with prompts; grade 5 (ss5-sourcing-corroboration) does it unprompted and uses it to weigh two accounts against each other. Students explain what each kind of source adds to an account of a voyage (D2.His.9): a ship's journal for dates and route, a map for what its maker knew, an object for daily life, a Native nation's oral history for what the landing meant to the people on shore. One task compares two sources on the same landing or site and notes what both confirm and where they differ, using the corroboration card from grades 2 and 3, with the check that the two did not copy each other.

words: explorer; expedition; empire; conquest; trade route; century
cross_subject: math:2.MD.B.6 (equally spaced points on a number line)
notes: Norse voyages and the evidence of their meetings with Native Peoples; European voyages of the 1400s and 1500s and why rulers paid for them (empire, routes to Asian trade, colonies, resources). Each voyage told with the Native nations it met, and conquest named plainly: Columbus's men enslaved Taíno people and their numbers collapsed from violence, forced labor and disease; Spanish soldiers with Native allies conquered the Mexica (Aztec) capital in 1521. Taíno descendants and Nahua people today. The class timeline of landings and conquests is drawn to scale in centuries, equal intervals for equal spans of time. Depth: D2.His.1 here compares events happening at the same time in different places; grade 3 ordered events on one line. Teacher note: conquest and enslavement named plainly with the human side; no role play of voyages or conquest.

words: territory; expansion; canal; railroad; frontier
notes: How the United States grew from 1791 to 1898 (the Louisiana Purchase, Oregon, the war with Mexico, Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico), mapped and dated on the timeline; canals, roads and railroads; why people moved west and what wagon-train life was like. Each gain told with the Native nations and the people of Mexico whose lands changed hands. Causes and effects of moving west, for movers and for the nations already there. Depth: D2.His.14 here links one cause to its effects; grade 5 (ss5-civil-war) weighs several causes of one event.

words: immigrant; enslaved; slavery; Civil War
notes: Many people came to the United States by choice; others, such as people from Africa, were brought by force and enslaved. By the mid 1800s the country was deeply divided over slavery and its spread into the West, which led to the Civil War (1861 to 1865). Teacher note: plain facts; people named as enslaved people; no role play or simulation.

words: independence; annex; treaty; border; Tejano; Californio
notes: Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California, Colorado, Utah and Nevada were part of Mexico. Texas declared independence in 1836, and the wish of many Anglo settlers to keep enslaved people, which Mexico had outlawed, was one cause; the United States annexed Texas in 1845, and the war with Mexico (1846 to 1848) ended with Mexico giving up about half its land. Told from Mexican, Tejano, Californio and Native sides as well as the US side; the people of Mexican descent who stayed and became US citizens. Teacher note: the war's causes are disputed then and now; show more than one account and the record that settles what can be settled.

words: region; statehood; admission; colony; territory; Pacific; Caribbean
cross_subject: math:4.NBT.B.4 (subtracting years to find spans)
notes: Locate the states of the five US regions (Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest, West) and the Caribbean and Pacific territories on a political map; build one class timeline of the dates each state joined, region by region; explain why being a state with its own constitution and a voice in Congress was better than being a British colony in the 1700s, and what a territory still lacks today (no voting member of Congress).

words: atlas; physical feature; resource; industry; landmark; national park; reservation
cross_subject: math:4.MD.A.2 (distances measured with the scale bar)
notes: Make a map of one state in each region from atlases and state websites, each with title, scale, compass rose and key: cities and capital, physical features, and one theme per region (resources and farming in the Midwest; climate, Native nations' homelands and reservations and early settlement in the Southwest; parks and historic sites in the West). Depth: D2.Geo.1 here builds a whole-state map with a chosen theme; grade 3 mapped a familiar place.

words: culture; heritage; immigrant; contribution; diverse; community
notes: Each region's peoples and what they built and gave: Native nations past and present, African Americans, Spanish and Mexican settlers, Europeans, Chinese, Japanese and later immigrants and recent arrivals, compared region by region, and why people moved where they did. Depth: D2.Geo.7 here compares movement into five regions over two centuries; grade 3 followed one set of trade routes. Teacher note: where a region's story includes it, exclusion and wartime incarceration (the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, Japanese American incarceration in World War II) are named plainly at grade level, beside what each group built.

words: natural resource; adapt; settlement; industry; specialize; trade
cross_subject: science:4-ESS3-1 (energy and fuels come from natural resources)
notes: Ask and research how people adapted to a region's environment, and how its rivers, coast, soil and resources shaped where towns grew and which industries and trade developed (the Northeast as the worked case, then compared with the other regions); why regions specialize in what they make and trade for the rest.

words: natural disaster; hurricane; tornado; drought; wildfire; flood; emergency; policy
cross_subject: science:4-ESS3-2 (reducing the impact of natural hazards); science:3-ESS3-1 (designs that reduce weather hazards)
notes: How hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, drought and wildfires have affected each region, how a disaster in one place affects people far away (prices, people who move), and how governments at each level and citizens responded: warnings, building rules, relief, volunteering. Students explain one response as a policy chosen to solve a public problem, and the challenges and new chances it brought. For one response students trace how the policy came about (D2.Civ.13): the disaster or problem that prompted it, who proposed it, how it was decided, and how it changed later (a building code tightened after a hurricane). Grade 4's yearly action cycle: students choose one local hazard from their research, find what their town or state already advises, and make one product for the school community (a family preparedness guide, a map of safe routes, a short talk to a younger class), checked against the official advice and shared through the school. Action is the students' choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks.

words: capital; Capitol; White House; Supreme Court; Congress; monument
notes: Washington, D.C. as the national capital: the Capitol, the White House and the Supreme Court as the buildings of the three branches (who works in each, named simply), and its monuments, museums and archives as civic resources anyone can use. That D.C.'s residents have no voting member of Congress is noted. Introduces the three branches by name only; grade 5 (ss5-constitution) teaches what each does and how they check each other.

words: trade; import; export; partner; interdependence
notes: Why the United States, Canada and Mexico trade so much with each other (each specializes, and trade lets each have more), what crosses the borders, and how trade helps some groups and hurts others in each country (a factory that grows, a farm that loses a market). Depth: D2.Eco.14 here explains why nations trade and who gains; grade 3 noticed that goods travel between countries. Named in grade 4 because its geography sets up the comparison; Massachusetts sets no economics standard at this grade.

words: colony; charter; land ownership; treaty
notes: English settlers and Native nations: disease, two different views of land, trade, the Pequot War and King Philip's War, told from English and Native sources; why different colonies were founded, with one founder researched; why English language and political ideas most shaped the later country. Teacher note: war and epidemic named plainly; the Wampanoag, Narragansett, Mashantucket Pequot and other nations of New England today.

words: region; climate; cash crop; labor; indentured servant
cross_subject: science:3-ESS2-2 (climates differ among regions)
notes: The 13 colonies on a map; how climate and land shaped crops and work in the New England, Middle and Southern colonies; the kinds of labor: family, hired, indentured and enslaved. Students read and make a map of the 13 colonies with a key for main crops and kinds of labor.

words: Middle Passage; enslaved; resistance; emancipation; petition; hired out; freedom suit
notes: Slavery legal in every colony through the 1700s and common among owners, many early leaders among them; the Atlantic trade and the Middle Passage; the lives of enslaved and free Africans; skills, families and the ways people resisted and sought freedom, including freedom suits (Elizabeth Freeman, Quock Walker) and Prince Hall's petitions; gradual emancipation in the North, and Massachusetts's courts ending slavery there by 1783. Teacher note: plain facts; no role play or simulation; enslaved people's own words where they exist. Builds on grade 3's Triangular Trade (ss3-sea-trade), now told with the Middle Passage and the people carried. Free and enslaved people compared directly (MA.5.T1.7a to d): enslaved people were held as property under law, could be sold away from their families, were denied schooling and punished for learning to read or for escaping, and these conditions led to revolts; many were skilled artisans whose owners hired them out and kept the pay; some gained freedom after service, by grant or by suing in court; free Black people in the North could marry, keep families, own property and work for wages, though with fewer rights than white neighbours. Handoff kind: from ss3-sea-trade (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: corroborate; perspective; claim; evidence
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.6 (several accounts of one event)
notes: Source each document before using it (who, when, for whom, why), then compare two accounts of one event, such as a Boston engraving of the 1770 shooting on King Street and a soldier's trial testimony; a written claim backed with evidence from two sources. Corroboration, met in grade 2 with two accounts, now weighs the accounts by their sources. Depth: D2.His.11 here infers audience and purpose unprompted and uses it to weigh the two accounts; grade 4 inferred them from one source with prompts.

words: tax; representation; boycott; protest; legislature; town meeting
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.3 (relationships between events in a historical text)
notes: Why Britain and France, each with Native allies, fought the French and Indian War (1754 to 1763) over the Ohio country, and how its debts led Britain to tax the colonies and the Proclamation of 1763 to close western land. Then British policies and colonial responses on the timeline (Sugar, Stamp, Townshend and Tea Acts, the Intolerable Acts); the slogan about taxation and representation; the Stamp Act Congress, the Sons of Liberty, the Boston Tea Party, the Suffolk Resolves, the fighting at Lexington, Concord and Bunker Hill, and the British leaving Boston in 1776; women's roles (boycotts and homespun cloth, writing for liberty, running farms and businesses while men were away, raising funds and supplying the Continental Army); colonial self-government (legislatures, town meetings, charters); a 1770s map of Boston with its sites and people, Crispus Attucks and Phillis Wheatley among them. The chain runs war, debt, taxes, protest, fighting.

words: Declaration of Independence; natural rights; Loyalist; Patriot; confederation; rebellion; inflation; deflation; unemployment
notes: The Declaration's argument and its ideas of equality, rights and the rule of law, and who those words left out in 1776; the later events on a map: the Battle of Trenton (December 1776, a river crossing and surprise win that kept the army together), the Battle of Saratoga (1777, the turning point that brought France in as an ally), the winter at Valley Forge (1777 to 1778, hunger, cold and training), and the siege of Yorktown (1781, which ended the major fighting), and why the Americans won; Loyalists and neutrals, and Native and African people who fought on both sides; leaders compared; the Articles of Confederation, why they were weak and failed, and Shays' Rebellion as a push toward the Constitutional Convention. Paper money that lost value (inflation) and farmers' debts are part of why Shays' Rebellion happened. After the war, hard money (coins) was scarce in states such as Massachusetts and prices fell (deflation), so a farmer's debt took more crops to repay, and many people could not find paid work (unemployment); students say who each change hurt. These postwar facts are checked by the day writer. Assumes grade 3's founding ideas across grade 4, which teaches no founding content. Handoff kind: from ss3-founding-ideas (grade 3) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: constitution; preamble; branch; checks and balances; compromise; amendment
cross_subject: ela:W.5.1 (opinion writing with reasons)
notes: The Preamble and the principles it holds; three branches and how each checks the others; what federal, state and local governments each do; the Convention's debates, including the Three-Fifths Compromise and how it kept the states together but strengthened slavery; voting and property rights not given to women; the Bill of Rights, with a claim backed by evidence about why one amendment was added in 1791. Depth: D2.Civ.3 here reads real constitutional provisions and asks why each was written; grade 3 asked what a rule is for. Assumes grade 3's founding ideas and levels of government across grade 4, which teaches only the capital's buildings. Depth: D2.Civ.1 completes here what grade 3 began: grade 3 named the levels of government, grade 5 adds the responsibilities of each branch. Handoff kind: from ss3-levels-of-government (grade 3) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by ss4-national-capital and ss4-disasters-response; from ss3-rules-rights (grade 3) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task; from ss3-founding-ideas (grade 3) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: president; term; cabinet; political party; precedent
notes: Washington, Adams and Jefferson: the main events of each term (the first cabinet, the first political parties and the peaceful handover of power in 1801, the Louisiana Purchase), judged by what each set out to do and what followed. Washington and Jefferson enslaved people and Adams did not, stated plainly as part of judging their leadership.

words: purchase; expedition; journal; interpreter; territory
cross_subject: math:5.G.A.1 (a coordinate grid)
notes: Why the Louisiana Purchase (1803) mattered, and the Lewis and Clark expedition (1803 to 1806) traced on a map with latitude and longitude from its journals, with Sacagawea (Lemhi Shoshone) and York, an enslaved man, named in it. The nations the expedition met (Mandan, Shoshone, Nez Perce and others) knew and governed that land; they live and govern today. The purchase bought France's claim, not the land of the nations who lived there. The route is described with compass directions (up the Missouri to the northwest, over the mountains west to the Pacific).

words: impressment; trade restriction; nationalism; anthem
notes: Causes of the War of 1812: British trade limits and the impressment of American sailors (and US hunger for western land); main events (the USS Constitution, the burning of the Capitol and White House, the Battle of New Orleans) and how the war built national pride. Tecumseh's alliance with Britain links to ss5-native-sovereignty-removal, taught later in the same grade (the columns hold only cross-grade links, so the link is kept here in words).

words: industry; textile mill; whaling; productivity; human capital; benefit; cost; pollution
cross_subject: science:5-ESS3-1 (communities protecting resources and environment)
notes: New England places of textile mills, machines, whaling, shipping and the China trade, on a map; how new machines and skills raised productivity and pay, how the region's work changed as it traded with near and far places, and the short- and long-term benefits and costs, including costs to people outside the deal (polluted rivers, dangerous mill work for young women and children). Northern mills spun cotton grown by enslaved people in the South, named plainly.

words: sovereignty; removal; treaty; Trail of Tears; resist
notes: 1800s conflicts between Native nations and governments over land and self-government: Tecumseh's call (1810) for nations to unite; Andrew Jackson and the Indian Removal Act of 1830; the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that Georgia's laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation, and the federal government's failure to enforce it; the Trail of Tears (1838), on which thousands of Cherokee people died, and the removal of the Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole nations; the Mashpee Revolt of 1833. Why people of the time differed, explained from their context. Present tense: the Cherokee Nation, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, the United Keetoowah Band, the other removed nations and the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe govern today, from their own materials. Teacher note: deaths and forced removal named plainly; no role play or reenactment of the march.

words: abolish; expand; internal slave trade; free state; slave state
notes: How Northern states ended slavery while it spread west and south with cotton; the 1808 ban on bringing enslaved people from abroad, and the trade inside the country that sold about a million people south and west and broke up families, until the 1860s; free and slave states on a map through the 1850s. Teacher note: family separation named plainly from enslaved people's own accounts; no role play or auction simulation.

words: abolitionist; Underground Railroad; narrative; petition; equality
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.8 (how an author uses reasons and evidence)
notes: People who fought slavery and worked for Black Americans' rights, Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth and others, Black and white, and the means they used (escape and the Underground Railroad, speeches, newspapers, petitions, the courts); read Douglass's own words and ask how his purpose shaped what he wrote. Teacher note: no escape simulation or Underground Railroad role play. Students then set those means beside ones people use today to change laws and protect rights (petitions, lawsuits, newspapers and online writing, peaceful marches), saying which earlier tactics are still used and what is new (D2.Civ.14).

words: secede; Union; Confederacy; cause; outcome; Reconstruction
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.3 (relationships between events in a historical text)
notes: The causes of the Civil War (slavery above all, fights over its spread west, the rise of the Republican Party) weighed from the seceding states' own declarations, which name slavery; the main leaders and battles (Grant, Lee, Gettysburg, Vicksburg) on a map and timeline; its outcomes, the end of slavery and Reconstruction. Summarize the argument of a short history written for young readers. Depth: D2.His.14 here weighs several causes of one event; grade 4 linked one cause to its effects. Teacher note: the claim that the war was not about slavery is checked against the seceding states' own words (values rule b); war deaths named plainly; no battle reenactment.

words: Emancipation Proclamation; amendment; citizenship; equal protection; Reconstruction
notes: Abraham Lincoln's part in building the Republican Party and his wartime choices; what the Emancipation Proclamation did and did not do; the 13th (ends slavery), 14th (citizenship and equal protection) and 15th (Black men's vote) Amendments, how each changed the law, and how Black Americans voted and held office during Reconstruction. How people changed the law, and how the law then changed lives.

words: suffrage; suffragist; vote; amendment; movement
notes: Women's rights work around the 14th and 15th Amendments (and the split over leaving women out) and its link to the later movement; the 19th Amendment (1920); that many women of color still could not vote in practice for decades after.

words: segregation; Jim Crow; discrimination; Black church; newspaper
notes: Black American life after Reconstruction under Jim Crow: segregation laws, limited jobs and schooling, voting blocked by poll taxes and tests, and white supremacist violence by the Ku Klux Klan and lynch mobs; and the Black churches, schools, organizations and newspapers that held communities together and pushed back. Teacher note: violence named plainly, with no photographs of victims and no slurs printed (rule 6); no role play.

words: research; compelling question; reliable; useful; argument; critique
cross_subject: ela:W.5.7 (short research project); ela:W.5.1 (opinion writing with reasons)
notes: Year-end research: each student or pair picks one 20th century person, group, event or law that widened civil rights (for African Americans, women, disabled people or others), writes its own supporting questions for a given compelling question, chooses sources and judges how useful each is from its maker, date and purpose, and writes a claim with evidence from several sources; classmates critique each argument. Depth: grade 5 writes its own supporting questions and finds its own evidence; grade 3 did both as a class. A counterclaim is not required: C3 places it in grades 6 to 8. Each topic's compelling question holds an idea open to more than one reading (what counts as winning a right), and students name two readings (D1.2); each supporting question lists the facts and ideas it needs (D1.3); and the source set is chosen to hold different views of the event, from supporters, opponents and the people affected (D1.5).

words: civil rights; movement; equality; disability rights; protest; law
notes: How the African American civil rights movement became a model for others: the women's movement, the disability rights movement (the 1977 sit-in for Section 504, the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990), Latino farmworkers, and the movement for LGBTQ people's equal treatment (the 1969 Stonewall uprising, and the Supreme Court's 2015 ruling that same-sex couples may marry). Teacher note: taught at grade level as a story of people seeking equal treatment under the law; court rulings stated as rulings (values rule a).

words: issue; strategy; predict; decision; action
notes: Once in the year, after the civil rights research: small groups name a school or local problem, compare two or three strategies people have used (from the year's history), predict what each would do, decide by an agreed process, and carry one out. Action is the students' evidence-based choice, never a cause the course picks. Depth: grade 5 plans in small groups and predicts results; grade 3 acted as a class with the teacher guiding. The decision step uses grade 3's deliberation (ss3-deliberation): restate the other view, give reasons, then decide by an agreed process. Handoff kind: from ss3-deliberation (grade 3) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: archaeologist; historian; geographer; economist; political scientist; discipline
notes: How each social science asks its own kind of question about one ancient place: the archaeologist asks what the objects and layers show, the historian what the written record says and who wrote it, the geographer why people settled there, the economist how people made and traded what they needed, the political scientist who held power and how. One site (for example a Mesopotamian city such as Ur) is looked at through all five, and students sort sample questions by field (C3: a question carries the key ideas of its field). Sets up the year: each region unit names which fields its evidence comes from. Students explain each sort: why this question belongs to that field (what it asks about and what evidence would answer it), not only where it goes.

words: interpretation; fossil; migration; dating; theory; revise
cross_subject: science:MS-LS4-1 (fossil record as evidence of change over time)
notes: Where and when modern humans arose in Africa and how groups spread to other continents, as a case of interpretation changing with evidence: finds such as Jebel Irhoud (Morocco), redated in 2017 to about 300,000 years, pushed back the earlier accepted date; new finds keep moving the dates of migration into Asia, Australia and the Americas. Students classify which kinds of sources a secondary account rests on (fossils, tools, genetic studies, dating methods) and say whether a newer view builds on, extends or rejects an older one, and where experts still disagree.
