Values rule (b): taught from the scientific record. Teacher note: some families hold faith accounts of human origins; the course teaches what the evidence shows and asks no student to state a belief. Students also weigh how much experts agree on each claim (most agree, a live debate, a single new finding) and say how that changes how sure a reader can be.

words: era; century; millennium; BCE; CE; circa; Ice Age
cross_subject: math:6.NS.C.5 (numbers on either side of a zero point); math:6.NS.C.7 (ordering on a line); science:MS-ESS1-4 (time scale of Earth history)
notes: The timeline grows from centuries to many thousands of years: era, century, millennium, BCE and CE, circa; why 3000 BCE is earlier than 2000 BCE (counting back from a zero point, like negative numbers); drawing a timeline to scale when spans run from 2.5 million years to a few thousand, using a long strip for deep time and a zoomed second strip for the last 12,000 years. The end of the last Ice Age (about 11,700 years ago) and the warming that made farming possible are placed on it. This timeline is the year's spine: every later unit adds to it. There is no year zero: the count runs 3 BCE, 2 BCE, 1 BCE, 1 CE, 2 CE, so from 2 BCE to 2 CE is 3 years, not 4; students check spans that cross the line by counting the years, not by plain subtraction. MA.6.T2.1 is taught as two separate objectives with their own checks: (1) place the large climate and environmental changes on the timeline (Ice Ages and the warming after them, changing coastlines and the greening and drying of the Sahara), and (2) explain how those changes allowed human life to spread and settle (land bridges opened, new plants and animals to hunt and gather, then farming). The scale timeline uses grade 4's equal spaces for equal spans (ss4-exploration). Handoff kind: from ss4-exploration (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: Paleolithic; Neolithic; domestication; nomadic; pastoral; shifting cultivation; artifact
notes: Paleolithic life (stone tools, fire, hunting and gathering, cave art such as Chauvet and Lascaux) and the Neolithic turn to farming, herding and metalworking about 10,000 years ago, in several places on their own (Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea, Africa). Three ways of farming life: settled villages, herding peoples who move with livestock, and farmers who clear and move on. Reintroduces the continuity-and-change chart for this course: students sort what changed and what stayed, and for whom (farming brought surplus and towns, and also more work, disease and inequality). Herding and shifting farming are not earlier steps on a ladder; they are ways of life many people still follow. Builds on ss4-first-peoples-evidence (grade 4); the handoff skips a grade because grade 5 is US history from the 1600s; archaeology as evidence was last taught in grade 4. Handoff kind: from ss4-first-peoples-evidence (grade 4) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: complex society; civilization; surplus; specialization; social class; stratified; monument
notes: The seven traits many scholars use to mark a complex society (food surplus, cities, social classes, specialized jobs, systems of government, religion and learning, monumental building and art, written or oral record keeping), taught as a debated working definition, not a ranking. How complex societies spread and meet others through trade, cultural exchange, migration, religious conversion, conquest and colonization. The trait list becomes a checklist used to compare every society met in grades 6 and 7. Teacher note: "civilization" was long used to rank peoples as more or less advanced; Curio Class uses "complex society", counts oral record keeping, and never ranks peoples.

words: latitude; longitude; absolute location; relative location; strait; peninsula; political map; physical map
cross_subject: math:6.NS.C.8 (points located by two signed coordinates)
notes: Map tools for the year, taught on Western Asia, the Middle East and North Africa: physical and political maps, the Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Bosporus, Suez Canal; countries, capitals and cities; absolute location by latitude and longitude (degrees north or south, east or west, like a coordinate grid with signs), relative location by direction and distance with the scale bar. Students use the map to add to a text they read. Carries latitude-longitude from grades 3 and 4 into degrees with signs.

words: arid; oasis; aquifer; population density; irrigation; resource
cross_subject: math:6.EE.C.9 (two related quantities on a climate graph); science:MS-ESS3-1 (uneven distribution of resources)
notes: Why people live where they do in the region today: rivers, coasts and oases in a mostly arid land, climate graphs, oil and water as resources, and dense river valleys beside nearly empty deserts. Satellite images and maps over time show environmental change (the drained and partly restored Mesopotamian marshes of Iraq, the Nile delta) and how people extend or pull back settlement as water and land change. The reasoning frame used for every region: location, landforms, climate and resources lead to settlement, population and economy. Each climate graph shows monthly temperature and rainfall for one city (a dependent quantity against the month), read as a pair of related quantities. Grade 6's yearly action cycle: students choose one local question of water or energy use from the region's lesson (how the school or town gets its water, or how much it uses), gather public facts, decide one small step the class can take or recommend, share it through the school, and look back at what changed. Action is the students' choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks.

words: Fertile Crescent; city-state; empire; Sumer; Babylon; Assyria
notes: How the Tigris and Euphrates floods and irrigation made farming and cities possible, and why the arc of farmland is called the Fertile Crescent; a map of archaeological sites with dates shows Sumerian city-states, then Babylonian and Assyrian empires, rising one after another, each placed on the class timeline. Students read the map and timeline together to say which came first and where.

words: surplus; productivity; specialization; innovation; irrigation; standard of living
notes: How irrigation, the plow, the wheel, the sail, metalworking and animal power let fewer farmers feed more people: productivity rose, a surplus freed others to become potters, scribes, smiths and traders, and towns grew. Economic reasoning grows from grade 5: each choice (dig a canal, keep a herd) has a cost, and higher productivity is why living standards can rise. Also who gained less: the work of building canals and the people at the bottom of the new order.

words: polytheism; ziggurat; priest; scribe; enslaved; relief sculpture; cylinder seal
notes: Mesopotamian society checked against the complex-society traits: rulers, priests, soldiers, craftspeople, farmers and enslaved people (often war captives or people sold for debt); many gods and the temple at the city's centre; ziggurats, relief sculpture, mosaics and cylinder seals read as evidence of who held power. Teacher note: slavery named plainly as part of this society, with no role play.

words: cuneiform; scribe; law code; stele; epic; justice
cross_subject: ela:RI.6.6 (an author's point of view and purpose)
notes: Cuneiform and what it was used for (records, taxes, laws, literature); the Epic of Gilgamesh in short translated passages; the Code of Hammurabi read as a source: who set it up, for whom, and why the king's prologue says the gods chose him to bring justice (a ruler's source tells his side). Students judge selected laws as answers to real problems (damaged canals, unpaid loans, building collapse), notice that penalties differed by social class, and write a short claim with evidence from the laws: was the code just, and for whom? The first full sourcing step of the year.

words: delta; cataract; upstream; downstream; flood plain; silt
notes: Upper Egypt is in the south and Lower Egypt in the north because the Nile flows north; students turn the map to read upstream and downstream, then place Nubia beyond the cataracts. Why the Nile mattered: yearly floods leaving silt, basin farming, a river road for trade, desert on both sides as protection; the flood cycle set the calendar.

words: pharaoh; dynasty; afterlife; mummification; hieroglyph; social pyramid
notes: The pharaoh as god and king and how royal art showed it; dynasties; at least one ruler studied closely (such as Hatshepsut or Ramses II); the social order from pharaoh and priests to scribes, artisans, farmers and enslaved people; religion, the afterlife, mummification and the gods. Perspective: royal art and tomb texts show the ruler's view, so students ask what they leave out. Teacher note: the Giza workers' town shows the pyramids were built mainly by paid and conscripted Egyptian laborers, not enslaved people as an old story says; slavery in Egypt is still taught plainly.

words: Old Kingdom; Middle Kingdom; New Kingdom; papyrus; calendar; pyramid
cross_subject: math:5.NBT.A.1 (place value, compared with Egyptian number writing)
notes: The Old, Middle and New Kingdoms placed on the timeline, each with its main achievements: farming systems, mathematics and surveying, astronomy and a 365-day calendar, papyrus and hieroglyphs (and how the Rosetta Stone let scholars read them), the Giza pyramids.

words: Nubia; Kush; Meroe; corroborate; bias; archaeology
notes: How we know about Kush: Egyptian records (often written by enemies or conquerors), Kush's own monuments and pyramids at Meroe, and its Meroitic script, still only partly read. Students find the limits of a record that is mostly written by outsiders, and compare Kush with Egypt: iron working, gold and trade, ruling queens (kandake), and the Kushite pharaohs who ruled Egypt as its 25th dynasty. Nubian peoples live in Sudan and southern Egypt today.

words: trade; merchant; colony; barter; currency; coin; entrepreneur
notes: The ancient Mediterranean on a map (Greece, Asia Minor, Crete, Phoenicia, the Aegean, the Red Sea); why Phoenicia's coast, cedar forests and harbors made it a sea-trading power from about 1000 to 300 BCE; purple dye and cedar as goods its land could make, founding colonies such as Carthage. Buyers and sellers, merchants taking risks to start ventures, and how trade moved from barter to weighed silver to coins (first struck in Lydia, about 600 BCE): money cuts the cost of finding someone who wants what you have. Who did the work: paid sailors and craftworkers beside enslaved rowers and laborers, and merchants who pooled their money or borrowed to fit out a voyage and shared the risk of losing a ship. Builds on grade 3's money and saving (ss3-money-saving); money was last taught in grade 3, since grades 4 and 5 carry no money content, so the unit opens with a short check on what money is for. Handoff kind: from ss3-money-saving (grade 3) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss3-money-saving.

words: alphabet; symbol; consonant; vowel; script; diffuse
notes: Three ways to write compared: cuneiform wedges, hieroglyphs, and the Phoenician alphabet of about 22 consonant letters; why an alphabet is easier to learn; how sea traders carried it, and how the Greeks added vowels and passed it toward Latin and the letters on this page. The geography reason: ships and trade routes spread ideas as well as goods. Students state what changed and what stayed after the alphabet spread (before: a few trained scribes and hundreds of signs; after: more people could write, while the old scripts lasted for some uses).

words: monotheism; covenant; Torah; Ten Commandments; temple; Hebrew Bible; diaspora
notes: The region on a historical map (Asia Minor, Greece, Mesopotamia, the Hittites, ancient Israel and Canaan, Egypt); the Hebrew Bible's account of Abraham, Moses and the Israelite tribes, the kingdom of Saul, David and Solomon, the first temple, its destruction and exile, and Roman rule to the destruction of the second temple in 70 CE. Judaism's ideas: one God, the Ten Commandments, the worth and responsibility of each person, and rulers bound by the same moral law as the ruled. Religion is taught as history: the scripture's account is named as its account ("the Hebrew Bible tells"), beside what archaeology shows where they differ. Jewish communities live and worship around the world today. Teacher note: no devotional practice is asked of students; place names are used as historians use them for each period, and the present-day conflict is not this unit's subject.

words: Christianity; messiah; gospel; apostle; New Testament; persecution
notes: Christianity's rise as a separate religion rooted in Judaism: Jesus's life and teachings as told in the New Testament, belief in him as messiah and in salvation, the Old and New Testaments, Paul's letters, and the faith's spread and growing variety across the Roman Empire, with periods of Roman persecution before Constantine. Taught as history, the scripture named as its account. Grade 7's Rome unit picks up the empire's side.

words: Islam; Muslim; Qur'an; prophet; Mecca; Medina; hijra
notes: Mecca and Medina on a map of the Arabian Peninsula; Muhammad's life (570 to about 632 CE), the hijra of 622, the Qur'an as the main source of Islamic belief; how Islam relates to Judaism and Christianity as monotheistic faiths that honor Abraham. Out of time order on purpose: the anchor groups the region's faiths together; grade 9 picks up the spread of Islam after 632. Taught as history, the Qur'an named as Muslims' account. Teacher note: Curio Class pages show no images of Muhammad, following widespread Muslim practice; no devotional practice is asked of students.

words: exchange; cultural diffusion; motif; conquest; route; Silk Roads
notes: How trade, cultural exchange and conquest linked the region's societies: goods, languages and art motifs moving along the Silk Roads and sea routes; Persian roads and Alexander's conquests as connectors. Students place one event inside the wider picture (a Phoenician colony, a new script, a conquest) and trace its causes and effects across places.

words: compelling question; supporting question; primary source; secondary source; significant; bibliography
cross_subject: ela:W.6.7 (short research project drawing on several sources)
notes: The first research project: one Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Phoenician, Israelite, early Islamic or Silk Roads society and a contribution to the modern world. Students write supporting questions that build the compelling one ("Why does this still matter?"), choose the kinds of sources each needs (at least one primary, one secondary), gather from several while checking origin and authority, and argue why the contribution is historically significant. A short written report with a source list; length and independence grow in grades 7 and 8. Students check whether their sources agree, revise the question when the evidence leads elsewhere, and test each source by its origin and authority before using it.

words: Sahara; Sahel; savanna; rain forest; desertification; projection; Great Rift Valley
cross_subject: science:MS-ESS3-3 (monitoring and lowering human impact on land)
notes: Africa's place, regions and features (the Sahara, Sahel, savanna and rain forest, Kilimanjaro, the Cape of Good Hope, the Great Rift Valley, Lake Victoria); its countries, capitals and cities by absolute and relative location. Map projections: why many wall maps shrink Africa and how an equal-area map shows its true size; paper and online maps compared. How landforms, climate (drought, desertification) and resources shape settlement and economies today, and long-term environmental change as a source of both conflict and cooperation (the Sahel's planting belt across many countries). Each student makes one simple electronic map with a free mapping tool (for example a map of rainfall or of one river's basin with a key) as well as reading the paper and online maps.

words: Axum; obelisk; Swahili; monsoon; port; Indian Ocean trade
notes: Axum (in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea): its Red Sea trade, coins, stone stelae, and its king's turn to Christianity in the 300s, which made Ethiopia one of the oldest Christian lands; East Africa's part in the spread of Christianity and later Islam. The Swahili coast's port towns linking inland Africa to Indian Ocean routes that reached South Asia and China, carried by monsoon winds; goods traded (gold, ivory, cloth, porcelain). Swahili is spoken by many millions in East Africa today. Teacher note: enslaved people were among the goods of Indian Ocean trade; named plainly.

words: trans-Saharan; caravan; empire; Ghana; Timbuktu; griot; Islam
notes: Ancient Ghana and the cities of the West African trade (Kumbi Saleh, Gao, and Timbuktu, which rose later as a center of trade and learning): gold from the south and salt from the Sahara, the camel caravan, rulers who taxed the trade; the spread of Islam with merchants; evidence from Arabic writers and from griots' oral histories. A cause-and-effect chain from the camel and gold to empire. Contributions: learning, trade networks, architecture. Teacher note: trade in enslaved people across the Sahara is named plainly; it is taught as its own system, neither used to excuse nor equated with the later Atlantic slave trade.

words: isthmus; archipelago; canal; hurricane; tropical; volcano
notes: Central America and the Caribbean on physical and political maps (the Gulf of Mexico, the Yucatan, the Panama Canal; present-day countries and major cities); how location, climate, volcanoes, hurricanes and resources shape settlement and economies. Students build their own map with a key showing one pattern (hurricane tracks, main crops or population), the first map they make from data this year.

words: Indigenous; Taino; Kalinago; Lenca; Miskito; descendant; territory
notes: The Taino, the Kalinago (called Carib by Europeans), the Lenca and the Miskito: ways of life tied to islands, coasts and highlands, and how land and sea shaped identity. Present tense as well as past, from each people's own published materials: the Kalinago Territory in Dominica, Taino descendant communities in Puerto Rico and elsewhere, the Lenca in Honduras and El Salvador, the Miskito in Nicaragua and Honduras. Teacher note: the Taino did not vanish, as older books say; the violence and disease of Spanish conquest are named plainly; sacred or restricted knowledge is left out. The unit opens by introducing these peoples as living nations and communities today, from their own pages, before their history. It uses grade 5's regional geography (ss5-colonial-regions: how climate and land shape ways of life) and grade 5's sourcing (ss5-sourcing-corroboration), since older European accounts of these peoples must be sourced for who wrote them and why.

words: Andes; Amazon; rain forest; altitude; terrace; deforestation
notes: South America's features (the Isthmus of Panama, the Andes, the Amazon, Cape Horn), countries and cities; how altitude, climate and resources shape where people live (coasts and highland valleys dense, the Amazon basin thin). How economic choices (farming, ranching, mining) change environments and lives near and far, with the Amazon's forest loss read from maps and data.

words: Maya; Andes; glyph; codex; Moche; Inca; limitation
cross_subject: ela:RI.6.9 (comparing two authors' presentations of events)
notes: A research report on one Mesoamerican society (such as the Maya) or Andean society (such as the Moche, Nazca or Inca): location, cities, farming, beliefs, writing or record keeping (Maya glyphs, Inca khipu). Students note what the evidence cannot show (Spanish clergy burned most Maya books; only four codices survive), use questions about their sources to find further ones, and write an explanation in the right order with details. The Maya did not disappear: millions of Maya people speak Maya languages in Guatemala, Mexico and Belize today, and Quechua and Aymara peoples live in the Andes, from their own materials. Builds on the grade 6 research project with a longer report.

words: subcontinent; monsoon; plain; Himalayas; population density; land use
cross_subject: science:MS-ESS2-6 (how unequal heating and the oceans shape climate)
notes: Central and South Asia on physical and political maps (the Indian Ocean, Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Ganges, Indo-Gangetic Plain, Himalayas); countries, capitals and cities by absolute and relative location. The monsoon and how it sets farming; how a very large and still-growing population changes land use (cities spreading over farmland). The grade 6 settlement frame applied with less support. Students also trace how people are moving within the region (from villages to cities, and across borders), and why.

words: Indus Valley; Harappa; Mohenjo-daro; seal; undeciphered; grid
notes: The Indus Valley cities (about 3000 to 1300 BCE): planned grids, drains, standard bricks and weights, long-distance trade with Mesopotamia. Its script is still unread, so students infer from other sources (where a seal was found, what it shows, Mesopotamian records of Meluhha) a plausible maker, date and use for objects whose origin is not stated. Builds on grade 6's Kush, where the record was written by outsiders. For each object students also ask who made it for whom: its origin and its audience (a seal used by traders, a figurine for the household), and how that shapes what it can show.

words: Hinduism; Vedas; dharma; karma; reincarnation; varna; caste; Dalit
notes: How Hinduism grew over many centuries from Vedic traditions, and its central ideas (dharma, karma, rebirth, many forms of the divine, the Vedas and Upanishads); about a billion Hindus practice it today, and it is taught from its own texts and practitioners, named as their account. How the caste system developed, and what continued and changed: the varna ideal and the many jatis, untouchability and discrimination against Dalits, outlawed by India's 1950 constitution and still an issue today. Teacher note: plain and fair; the arrival of Indo-Aryan language speakers is taught as a scholarly question with its evidence, not as an old "invasion" story; no student is asked about their own family's caste or faith. The continuity-and-change chart comes from grade 6 (ss6-paleolithic-neolithic). The comparison with grade 6's Judaism (ss6-ancient-israel) stays a content connection: students set one idea of each faith beside the other, each told from its own texts.

words: Buddhism; enlightenment; Four Noble Truths; nonviolence; edict; empire
notes: Siddhartha Gautama's teachings (Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path) in the 6th to 4th centuries BCE; the Mauryan Empire and Ashoka, who turned to Buddhist teaching and nonviolence after the bloody Kalinga war; the Gupta Empire. Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts as sources: who carved them, for whom, and how useful they are for knowing his rule versus his subjects' lives. Builds on grade 6's reading of Hammurabi's stele (a ruler's own words).

words: zero; decimal; place value; astronomy; stupa; Ajanta
cross_subject: math:5.NBT.A.1 (place value in base ten)
notes: Achievements of ancient India: the place-value numerals with zero later carried west by Arab scholars, astronomy and mathematics (Aryabhata), medicine, the stupa at Sanchi and the Ajanta cave paintings, metalwork such as the Delhi iron pillar.

words: supply; demand; scarcity; middleman; toll; barrier; caravan
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.3c (price rises given as a percent)
notes: How geography made the Silk Roads workable (oases, passes, steppe) and costly (deserts, mountains); India's and Central Asia's links to East Africa, Western Asia and Europe by conquest, trade, colonies and the spread of religion and language; China's part, and Buddhism reaching China from about the 1st century CE. Introduces the supply-and-demand graph: why silk sold so dear in Rome (scarce supply, strong demand, many middlemen each taking a share, competition among them), and how tolls, war and bandits acted as barriers that raised prices and cut trade. Prices of skilled work too: guides who knew the routes and languages were paid well because few could do it. Coins from different lands were changed at a rate, and lenders charged traders more on dangerous roads, where the risk of losing the goods was higher.

words: compare; contrast; parallel timeline; development; dynasty
notes: The comparison skill of the year: key economic, political and religious developments in India and China set on parallel timelines beside grade 6's Mesopotamia and Egypt, judged with the complex-society traits from grade 6 and with each region's environment. Students write how two societies were alike and unlike and why (river floods, mountains, trade position), not which was "better".

words: Huang He; Chang Jiang; plateau; loess; isolation; terrace
notes: East Asia on physical and political maps (the Huang He and Chang Jiang, the Himalayas, the Gobi and Taklamakan, the North China Plain); countries, capitals, cities. How mountains, deserts and seas set China somewhat apart and how its rivers and loess soils supported early farming, and how geography shapes where people live and work there today.

words: dynasty; oracle bone; Mandate of Heaven; Confucius; filial piety; Taoism
notes: The Shang and Zhou (about 1600 to 256 BCE): oracle bones as the earliest Chinese writing and a source, bronze, the Mandate of Heaven and the dynastic cycle as a continuity-and-change pattern. Confucius on ethics, good government, proper conduct and family and social bonds (from short translated sayings of the Analects); Taoism and harmony with nature. Both are still practiced and taught today.

words: unify; Legalism; standardize; Great Wall; character; bronze casting
notes: The First Emperor and the short Qin dynasty (221 to 206 BCE): conquest, a central government, strict Legalist rules, one set of weights, coins and script, and huge state projects (early walls, roads, his tomb and terracotta army) built by forced and conscripted labor. Chinese characters stand for words and ideas, unlike the alphabet from grade 6. Technologies: bronze casting, silk, and later paper and gunpowder. Teacher note: forced labor and the burning of books named plainly.

words: diffusion; Korea; Japan; Shinto; Silla; Heian; Zen
notes: Buddhism's spread from India to China, Korea and Japan, traced on a map and timeline; its growth in Japan from the 6th to the 13th century; ancient Japan's contributions (Shinto shrines, the Heian court, The Tale of Genji, poetry). Trade, religion and conquest among China, Korea and Japan. Chronology: this topic runs past 500 CE because the anchor follows Buddhism's spread; grade 9 picks up the rest of the world from about 500.

words: Oceania; atoll; archipelago; outback; Antarctica; Pacific Islands
notes: The Indian and Pacific Oceans, Australia, New Zealand, Antarctica and the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia, on physical and political maps; how location, landforms, climate and resources shape settlement (Australia's dry interior and coastal cities, crowded river deltas of Southeast Asia, small islands). Students compare two places to say what makes them alike and different, using both culture and environment. Builds on grade 6's map projections (polar regions and the Pacific look very different on different maps).

words: Aboriginal; Torres Strait Islander; Maori; rock art; oral tradition; Polynesian voyaging
notes: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia, with one of the longest continuous cultures on Earth (rock art and sites tens of thousands of years old), and the Maori of New Zealand, who arrived by Polynesian voyaging about 1300 CE. Social features, kinship and land, and what rock art and oral tradition show. Present tense as well as past, from the peoples' own published materials (Aboriginal land councils, Maori iwi). Teacher note: use "Aboriginal peoples" rather than the older "Aborigines"; some communities ask that images of people who have died and sacred sites not be shown; sacred or restricted knowledge left out.

words: peninsula; plain; Alps; Danube; Rhine; Mediterranean climate
notes: Europe on physical and political maps (the Mediterranean, North and Baltic Seas, the Danube, Rhine, Alps, Pyrenees, the North European Plain); countries, capitals and cities; how a long coastline, navigable rivers and a mild climate shaped settlement and economies. Students make a map of Europe's rivers and mountains with a key.

words: time zone; prime meridian; Greenwich; International Date Line; chronometer
cross_subject: math:7.NS.A.1 (adding and subtracting signed numbers); science:5-ESS1-2 (Earth turning gives day and night)
notes: Time zones as slices of longitude (Earth turns 15 degrees an hour); the prime meridian at Greenwich and why it was chosen; the International Date Line; how sailors once measured longitude by comparing local time with an accurate clock. Students work out the time in other cities from offsets. A modern topic placed here by the anchor with Europe's geography.

words: city-state; colony; Aegean; Peloponnese; Hellenistic
notes: Greece on a historical map of the Mediterranean and how far its influence reached from about 1200 to 300 BCE; why mountains split Greece into city-states and why Athens, Corinth, Sparta and others turned to the sea for trade and planted colonies from Spain to the Black Sea.

words: polis; democracy; assembly; citizen; jury; rule of law; constitution
notes: Democratic ideas from ancient Greece: the polis, the assembly and council, voting and selection by lot, juries, written laws and the rule of law. Who counted: adult male citizens only; women, enslaved people and foreign residents were shut out. Students compare direct democracy with representative government, set up for grade 8's roots of US government. Students run one structured class deliberation under assembly rules (a speaker's turn, a time limit, a vote) on a question from their own school. Grade 7's yearly action cycle grows from it: the class chooses one school issue, deliberates under those rules, decides an action (a letter to the principal or a proposal to the student council), carries it out through the school and looks back on the result. Action is the students' choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks. Depth: D2.Civ.9 runs one procedure here; grade 8 compares deliberative procedures.

words: oligarchy; helot; status; perspective; citizen
notes: Life in Athens and Sparta compared, including the roles and status of women and of enslaved people (Athenian household and mine slaves, Sparta's helots held in subjection by force). Students explain the factors (wealth, war, law, religion) that shaped how people of each city saw the world, without adopting those views. Teacher note: plain facts; no role play.

words: Persian Wars; Peloponnesian War; alliance; Alexander the Great; Hellenistic
notes: Causes and results of the Persian Wars, the Peloponnesian War and Alexander's conquests in Asia. Students weigh causes, not just list them: Thucydides judged Athens' growing power and Sparta's fear the truest cause of the Peloponnesian War; students rank causes and defend the ranking.

words: myth; god; goddess; hero; allusion
cross_subject: ela:L.6.4 (word meaning from context and roots)
notes: Greek gods, goddesses, heroes and stories in short retellings, and why words and phrases from them (Pandora's box, Herculean, panic, echo) are still used. Myths taught as the beliefs and stories of the ancient Greeks.

words: credible; relevant; secondary work; argument; revise
cross_subject: ela:W.7.7 (short research projects from several sources)
notes: Research and report on one area of Greek accomplishment (a scientist or mathematician, a writer or thinker, architecture, the alphabet with vowels, or art). New this year: judging whether a source is credible and fits the question, comparing the central arguments of two secondary works (an article and a video, say), and critiquing a classmate's explanation for its order and support before revising. Longer and more independent than grade 6.

words: republic; senate; consul; tribune; veto; separation of powers; civic duty
notes: Rome's location on a map and the empire's growth to about 500 CE; the Roman Republic: consuls, senate, assemblies and tribunes, the veto, written law (the Twelve Tables), separation of powers, representative government and civic duty. Students match Roman offices to the branch idea from grade 5, which grade 8 carries into the US system. Builds on ss5-constitution (grade 5); the handoff skips a grade because the grade 6 course (ancient Western Asia, Africa and the Americas) has no topic on how a government is structured. The branches card from grade 5 returns with a short retrieval task before the Roman case. Handoff kind: from ss5-constitution (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: dictator; emperor; legion; province; administration
notes: How Julius Caesar and Augustus turned the Republic into an empire, and why the empire grew and lasted: an organized army, conquest, and provinces run with local leaders. Placed on the timeline.

words: tax; currency; inflation; Pax Romana; trade policy; customs duty; deflation
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent increase and tax rates)
notes: What Roman taxes paid for (the army, roads, grain for Rome) and who paid; one currency, roads and protected sea lanes helping trade grow under the Pax Romana; customs duties on trade and who gained and lost from them. Inflation: when later emperors cut the silver in coins, prices rose, hurting people on fixed pay and savings more than landowners. Supply and demand from the Silk Roads row applied to money itself. Deflation and joblessness also struck: in 33 CE money became scarce, loans were called in, land prices fell and many lost their property until the emperor lent money interest-free (the day writer checks this case). Students compare who is hurt when prices rise and who when prices fall. The budget card from grade 3 (ss3-money-saving) returns here for a public budget; a short reteach opens the lesson.

words: patrician; plebeian; enslaved; freedman; revolt; manumission
notes: Rome's classes (patricians, plebeians, freed people) and slavery: millions enslaved by conquest, birth and debt, in households, farms and mines; revolts such as Spartacus's; freeing by owners and the limits on freed people. Sources where enslaved and freed people's own voices survive (tombstones). Teacher note: plain facts; no role play.

words: decline; corruption; invasion; division; transformation; counterclaim
cross_subject: ela:W.7.1 (argument with claims and evidence)
notes: Internal causes (corruption, civil wars, a weak economy and inflation) and external ones (invasions, shrinking trade) of the Western empire's breakup by 476 CE, while the Eastern empire lasted another thousand years. Students build a multi-cause explanation and take a side in the historians' debate (a fall, or a slower transformation), with evidence. Grade 7 ends here, about 500 CE; grade 9 World History picks up from 500. Counterclaim is taught here as a word and a move: students state the strongest point for the other side of the debate and answer it with evidence.

words: aqueduct; arch; concrete; engineering; amphitheater
notes: Roman roads, aqueducts, arenas, baths, plumbing, the arch and concrete, and which still stand or shape building today.

words: Latin; Romance languages; root; prefix; suffix
cross_subject: ela:L.7.4 (Greek and Latin roots as clues to meaning)
notes: How the Roman alphabet and Latin spread with the empire into the Romance languages, and how Latin and Greek roots build scientific and school words today (students take apart words such as "aqueduct", "biology", "democracy").

words: diffusion; migration; colonization; exchange
notes: The year's closing look: how scientific, philosophical and artistic ideas moved across Europe, Asia and Africa by trade, migration, conquest and colonization (Greek ideas carried east by Alexander, Buddhism west and east, Roman law and Latin across Europe), mapped on one world map.

words: democracy; republic; jury; rule of law; separation of powers
notes: Why the founders looked to Athens and Rome: voting, juries and the rule of law from Athens; the Republic's separation of powers and civic duty. Students trace each idea to where it shows in US government and where the founders chose otherwise (representation instead of direct democracy). Recalls grade 7 directly.

words: Enlightenment; natural rights; social contract; Magna Carta; habeas corpus; legislature
notes: Locke on natural rights and government by consent; Montesquieu on separating powers; the Magna Carta, habeas corpus, Parliament and the English Bill of Rights; colonial legislatures and town meetings as self-government practice. Short excerpts read in plain words, placed on the timeline.

words: Haudenosaunee; confederacy; Great Law of Peace; sovereignty; counterclaim
cross_subject: ela:RI.8.8 (judging whether evidence is enough to support a claim)
notes: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora) and its Great Law of Peace, from the Confederacy's own published materials; it still governs today, with its Grand Council at Onondaga. Students weigh the evidence for the claim that it influenced US government (Franklin's Albany Plan remarks, the 1988 congressional resolution) against historians' counterclaims, and say what each side's evidence can and cannot show. Teacher note: Native nations in the present tense; sacred or restricted knowledge left out.

words: Declaration of Independence; equality; natural rights; consent; grievance
notes: What led colonists to declare independence (from grade 5), then the Declaration read closely as a source: its argument, its claims of equality and natural rights, government by consent and limited, representative government; who those words left out in 1776 (enslaved people, women, Native nations) and how later movements used them. Jefferson's cut passage on the slave trade as evidence of the debate. Builds on ss5-revolution-causes (grade 5) and ss5-independence-war (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Handoff kind: from ss5-revolution-causes (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task; from ss5-independence-war (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: Articles of Confederation; Shays' Rebellion; convention; compromise; Three-Fifths Compromise; delegate
notes: Why the Articles failed (no power to tax, no executive, one vote per state), Shays' Rebellion, and the Convention: its leaders, and the debates over power, rights, representation (the Great Compromise) and slavery (the Three-Fifths Compromise, the slave-trade clause, the fugitive slave clause) and how each was settled. Teacher note: plain facts on how the Constitution protected slavery. Builds on ss5-constitution (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Handoff kind: from ss5-constitution (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: ratify; Federalist; Anti-Federalist; federalism; checks and balances
notes: The Federalist and Anti-Federalist cases on ratifying the Constitution (federalism, checks and balances, limited government, a bill of rights) from short excerpts of each; students explain each side's fears and hopes and why the Bill of Rights became the bargain.

words: Preamble; article; amendment; Bill of Rights; ratify
notes: The Preamble, each of the seven articles in plain words, and the Bill of Rights, with why it was added in 1791; the purposes and impact of a constitution compared with other founding agreements (a treaty, a charter). Builds on ss5-constitution (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Handoff kind: from ss5-constitution (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: legislative; executive; judicial; checks and balances; veto; agency
notes: Congress, the President and executive agencies, and the federal courts: what each does, its powers and limits, and how each checks the others (veto and override, confirmation, judicial review, impeachment); party leaders in Congress. Compared briefly with a parliamentary system in another country.

words: necessary and proper clause; elastic clause; implied power; judicial review; appeal; dissent
notes: The necessary and proper ("elastic") clause and implied powers, with McCulloch v. Maryland; judicial review from Marbury v. Madison (1803); how a case reaches the Supreme Court, is argued and decided, and why dissents matter.

words: election; primary; Electoral College; nominate; confirm; political party; interest group
notes: How members of Congress and the President are elected (primaries, general elections, the Electoral College) and how judges and executive officials are nominated and confirmed; the roles of parties in state and national elections; how citizens take part through elections, parties and interest groups, and the separate powers and duties of each, and of the media.

words: campaign finance; advertisement; turnout; poll; source
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percents in turnout and polling data)
notes: Evaluating election information: candidates' positions from their own statements, campaign finance records, ads and media coverage, voter turnout data by age and year. Sourcing each item (who paid for it, what it wants you to do). Examples drawn from several parties and from past elections; students never say whom they or their families support.

words: citizen; naturalization; birthright; jury duty; resident; civic life; private life
notes: Ways to become a US citizen (birth, naturalization); the rights and duties of citizens (voting, jury duty, taxes, holding office) compared with those of non-citizens; civic, political and private life told apart. Builds on grade 7's who-counted-as-a-citizen in Athens. Teacher note: classes include non-citizens and mixed-status families; no question asks about a student's or family's status.

words: liberty; equality; common good; justice; due process; popular sovereignty; minority rights
notes: Core civic values with examples, and the tensions between them: liberty and equality or authority, individual rights and the common good, majority rule and minority rights. Students explain how personal interests and perspectives meet shared principles on a real issue, and hear more than one view.

words: leadership; public service; delegate; trustee; political courage
notes: What good leadership looks like and how to judge leaders at community, state and national levels by evidence; why citizens work with elected leaders; careers in public service; the delegate and trustee views of a representative; leaders who showed political courage and those who fell short of Constitutional ideals, from more than one party and era.

words: protest; petition; boycott; civil disobedience; assembly
notes: The role of protest in a democracy, protected by the First Amendment, and past and present ways of changing society (petitions, boycotts, marches, lawsuits, voting drives, lobbying), with cases from across the political spectrum. What changed and what stayed between eras.

words: interest group; lobbying; think tank; nonprofit; labor union; corporation; public policy
notes: How public and private interest groups, policy research organizations, labor unions, businesses and nonprofits shape debate on public policy, and their roles in the economy; one policy traced from problem to law to results, with who gained and who paid.

words: secession; amendment; Reconstruction; equal protection; suffrage
notes: The Constitutional issues that led to the Civil War (slavery and its spread, states' claims against federal power, secession), shown from the secession declarations, which name slavery; how the war and the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments grew federal power and individual rights; the 19th (1920) and 26th (1971) Amendments in their context. Teacher note: slavery named plainly as the central cause. Builds on ss5-reconstruction-amendments (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Builds on ss5-civil-war (grade 5) for the war's events. Handoff kind: from ss5-civil-war (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task; from ss5-reconstruction-amendments (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: civil rights; Civil Rights Act; Voting Rights Act; disability rights; discrimination
notes: The 1964 Civil Rights Act, the 1965 Voting Rights Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990): their context, what they did and the movements behind them; how and why views of human and civil rights changed over time, including court rulings that extended rights to new groups (such as same-sex marriage in 2015). Builds on ss5-civil-rights-movements (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Handoff kind: from ss5-civil-rights-movements (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: precedent; majority opinion; dissent; overrule; First Amendment; equal protection
cross_subject: ela:W.8.1 (argument with claims, counterclaims and evidence); ela:W.8.7 (research projects)
notes: Research and report, orally or in writing, on one area where Supreme Court decisions changed citizens' lives: First Amendment freedoms (Tinker v. Des Moines), due process and equal protection (from Dred Scott v. Sandford to the 14th Amendment and later cases), or rights against community interests (the flag salute cases, where Barnette overruled Gobitis). An argument from the opinions and other sources that names its limits. Values rule (a): where the Court later overruled itself, the later ruling stands. Teacher note: Dred Scott's language is summarized, not printed; Jehovah's Witness families' persecution named plainly. The year's longest research piece.

words: federalism; enumerated power; implied power; reserved power; Tenth Amendment; state constitution
notes: Federalism for the student's own state: what state and national governments each do; provisions of the US Constitution and the state's constitution that define and divide powers; enumerated versus implied powers; the Tenth Amendment and the powers and limits it sets. Written for any state; Massachusetts (1780) serves as one worked example of a state constitution. Builds on ss5-constitution (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Handoff kind: from ss5-constitution (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: declaration of rights; Bill of Rights; 14th Amendment; protection
notes: The Bill of Rights, the 14th Amendment and the student's state constitution's declaration of rights compared; protections the state constitution gives that the US Constitution does not (state constitutions often add rights such as education or privacy). Students find and read their own state's text.

words: governor; state legislature; state supreme court; county; mayor; council; town meeting; school board
notes: Federal, state and local duties contrasted (rights, police, welfare, schools); the student's state government: governor and agencies, legislature, state courts up to the highest court; local government (counties, cities, towns with councils, mayors, select boards or town meetings, school boards, sheriffs and local courts). How decisions are made at each level compared with a classroom or school. Written for any state. Builds on ss5-constitution (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Students also say what each procedure is for (a public hearing lets people be heard; a two-thirds rule protects the minority) and whether it does that job. Handoff kind: from ss5-constitution (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

hands_on: econ-taxes-budgets; econ-scarcity-choice; econ-earning-income; us2-econ-toolkit; econ-incentives; econ-saving-interest
words: tax; public good; budget; bond; interest rate; unemployment; revenue; GDP; inflation; spillover
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percents in tax and interest)
notes: Tax-supported services of state and local government (schools, roads, parks, libraries, public safety) and why some goods are paid for in common (benefits and costs that spill over to others); a real state or town budget read for its trade-offs; borrowing through bonds and how higher interest rates make a new school or road cost more; employment and growth data and how a slowdown cuts tax revenue. Students weigh two solutions to a local budget question for different groups. Builds on grade 7's Roman taxes. Two measures read from one state chart: inflation (how fast prices rise) and GDP (the value of everything made in a year), and what each says about the state's economy. Spillovers shown on a supply-demand graph: when a good's costs fall on others (pollution) or its benefits spill to others (vaccination), the market makes too much or too little, which is one reason government taxes, pays for or regulates it.

words: free press; censorship; First Amendment; prior restraint
notes: Why press freedom is protected in the First Amendment and in the student's state constitution (Massachusetts's Article 16 as an example): publishing without government control or censorship; how a free press offers competing information and views on government.

words: news article; editorial; op-ed; editorial cartoon; credibility; misinformation; lateral reading
cross_subject: ela:RI.8.6 (author's point of view and how it is shown)
notes: The purposes of news articles, editorials, editorial cartoons and op-eds; benefits and problems that digital news and social media bring to democracy; checking information: who is behind it, what other sources say (reading across sites), claims and evidence. Builds on grade 7's judging sources for credibility.

words: point of view; claim; evidence; bias; credibility
cross_subject: ela:RI.8.8 (judging an argument's reasoning and evidence)
notes: Analyze the point of view and judge the claims of an editorial, cartoon or op-ed on a local, state or national policy issue, with pieces from more than one side on the same issue; students critique an argument's credibility, not its side.

words: deliberation; informed action; stakeholder; proposal; audience
cross_subject: ela:SL.8.1 (collaborative discussion)
notes: Names no Massachusetts code: it carries the C3 action indicators the year's civics content needs. Once a year: students deliberate on a school or community problem, look at it at local, regional and global levels, weigh what they can do and the levers available, choose an action themselves (a letter to an official, a presentation to a school board, a public report), and present to an audience beyond the class. Action is the student's choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks. Builds on ss5-informed-action (grade 5); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 6 and 7 are world geography and ancient civilizations; grade 8 is the civics year. Depth: D2.Civ.9 in grade 7 ran one deliberation procedure; grade 8 compares deliberative procedures (assembly rules, a town meeting, a consensus circle) and judges which suits which question. Grade 8 builds on the grade 6 and 7 action cycles. Handoff kind: from ss5-informed-action (grade 5) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by ss6-mena-settlement and ss7-athenian-democracy.

words: compelling question; supporting question; enduring issue; source type
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.7 (short research projects driven by a question)
notes: Build the inquiry for a unit: a compelling question that names an enduring issue of world history (Did trade or conquest do more to connect the world before 1500? What makes a ruler's power legitimate?), supporting questions that break it into day-sized parts, and a plan for which kinds of sources could answer each (chronicle, map, object, law code, travel account), noting whose view each kind of source carries and whose it leaves out. Grade 9 depth: students draft the supporting questions for a given compelling question and see how a source read on day 2 raises a new question by day 4. Grade 10 adds the disagreement among historians (wh2-contested-questions).

words: primary source; provenance; audience; purpose; artifact; inscription
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.6 (author purpose and point of view)
notes: Read many kinds of primary sources as evidence: texts, maps, diagrams, art and buildings (a mosaic of Justinian's court, a Mali court record told by a visiting scholar, a Song scroll, a portolan chart). Before using any source, students judge its usefulness for this question from maker, date, place, audience and purpose, and they gather a set of sources that holds more than one view. Grows the grade 6 to 8 sourcing habit into a judgment of fitness: a biased source can still be good evidence of what its maker believed. Every source is put through five checks: origin (who made it, when, where), authority (how they could know), structure (what kind of source it is and how it is built), context (what was happening around it), and corroborative value (what other independent sources confirm it).

words: parallel timeline; thematic map; trade route; comparison chart; scale
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.3 (scaled bar graphs); ela:RI.9-10.7 (information in different media)
notes: Make graphic displays that show interaction and comparison: maps of physical features, borders, trade routes and invasions (MA.WHI.T1.5a); parallel timelines that put empires rising and falling in different regions side by side on one scale (T1.5b); charts and bar graphs comparing population or the value of traded goods (T1.5c). Students make the display and then use it to support a claim. Taught early in the year and used in every later unit; the parallel timeline is the year's spine. Builds on ss7-comparing-societies (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. The map scale, latitude and longitude, and region cards from grades 3 to 7 open with a short retrieval task. words: interaction; exchange; migration; alliance; colonization; conquest
notes: The bridge from grade 7, which ends about 500 CE: the ways societies interact (trade, the spread of ideas, migration, exploration, alliance, colonization, conquest), shown first with exchanges among ancient societies up to about 500 (Han China and Rome along the overland routes, Indian Ocean monsoon trade, Bantu-speaking migrations in Africa). Recap of grade 7 content is brief; the new skill is classifying an interaction and naming who gained and who lost by it. Students explain an interaction as a two-way system: geography shapes trade, and trade changes the land (irrigation, deforestation, new crops). The reasoning grows from grade 6 and 7 location work to explaining why there and so what. Each faith is described as its own followers describe it, in the present tense, since each is practised by many millions today. Teacher note: conversion by force and by choice are both in the record; name each where the sources show it. words: indigenous religion; ancestor; syncretism; oral tradition; diviner
notes: Indigenous religious practice in Africa (ancestors, a creator and lesser spirits, diviners and healers, oral tradition) and how it survived and shaped African Christianity and Islam, for example in Ethiopia's church and in West African Islam. Present tense as well as past: Yoruba orisa traditions, Vodun in Benin and the Akan traditions are practised today in Africa and the Americas, and are described from their communities' own published materials. Sacred or restricted knowledge is left out. Teacher note: avoid words like primitive or animist as labels; use the names communities use.

words: caliphate; patronage; legal code; tolerance; golden age
notes: One empire of about 100 to 1000 CE studied for how political power, religion and culture fed each other: the Gupta or Kushan Empire, the early Byzantine Empire (Constantinople, Hagia Sophia, Justinian's code), or the Abbasid Caliphate (Baghdad's scholarship). Each student or group takes one option in depth and the class hears all three, so the course meets the standard's one-empire rule and still compares. The historical skill is context: students explain why a policy (toleration, a law code, patronage of scholars) made sense in its time and place and in the wider world of its century. Builds on ss7-rome-fall (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-rome-fall (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: hereditary rule; dynasty; kingdom; empire; feudal society; legitimacy
notes: The words for political power used through the rest of the year: hereditary rule, dynasty, kingdom, empire and feudal society, and why each matters when comparing power across places and times (a dynasty can rule an empire; feudal ties bind lords and vassals by land and service). Students sort later examples (Song, Mali, Kamakura Japan, France) by these terms and ask whose view of a ruler's legitimacy a source records. Reintroduces the perspective model for this course in a civics frame: rulers, subjects and outsiders saw the same power differently.

words: gold-salt trade; caravan; city-state; griot; Swahili; mosque university
notes: Opens the kingdoms and empires of 1000 to 1500 (MA.WHI.T3.2 asks students to map one and explain its politics, economy, culture and links to other regions; its options run across this row and wh1-silk-roads-mongols, wh1-song-kamakura, wh1-ottoman-mughal, wh1-american-empires, wh1-european-kingdoms and wh1-italian-city-states, and each student maps one in depth). Ghana, Mali and Songhai: the gold and salt trade across the Sahara, Mansa Musa, Timbuktu as a centre of trade and learning (its manuscripts), and the trade in enslaved people alongside gold. Axum, or the Swahili city-states of the East African coast and their Indian Ocean trade. Sources include Arabic travellers' accounts and the oral tradition of griots, compared. Present tense: Mali and Ghana are nations today, Timbuktu's manuscript families still keep their collections, and Swahili is spoken by many millions. Teacher note: the slave trade is named plainly as part of the economy. Builds on ss6-west-africa-trade (grade 6) and ss6-axum-swahili (grade 6); the handoff skips 2 grades because grade 7 covers South and East Asia, Oceania and Europe and grade 8 is civics; this region's history resumes in grade 9 world history.
