words: Silk Roads; khan; nomad; tribute; travel account; Pax Mongolica
notes: The Mongol Empire: Chinggis (Genghis) and Khubilai (Kublai) Khan, conquest and its destruction, then the protected trade on the Silk Roads, contact with Europeans, and Yuan and early Ming China. The goods that moved in every direction (horses, grain, furs, spices, silk, paper) and how travellers' accounts and maps added to what people knew of the world (Ibn Battuta, Marco Polo, Rabban Sauma, later Zheng He's voyages). Students source each travel account: what could this traveller have seen, and for whom did he write? Builds on ss7-silk-road-trade (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-silk-road-trade (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: scholar-official; civil service exam; Neo-Confucianism; shogun; samurai; Zen
notes: Song Dynasty China (the scholar-official chosen by examination, landscape painting and calligraphy, the blending of Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian thought, a commercial economy with paper money) and the Kamakura Shogunate in Japan (military rule by the shogun and samurai, the failed Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281, Buddhist sculpture and Zen-influenced art). Builds on grade 7 ancient China and Japan. The comparison is the skill: two East Asian states of the same centuries, one governed by examined officials, one by warriors. Builds on ss7-buddhism-east-asia (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-buddhism-east-asia (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: sultan; janissary; millet; gunpowder empire; textile; miniature painting
notes: The Ottoman Empire from 1299 through the fall of Constantinople in 1453 to Suleiman I, including how it governed many peoples and faiths (the millet system) and the janissaries, boys taken by levy from Christian families; and the early Mughal Empire in India, a great exporter of textiles, ships and firearms and a centre of illustrated manuscripts. Students compare how the two ruled religiously mixed populations. Teacher note: the levy of Christian boys (devshirme) is named plainly, with what it meant to the families.

words: city-state; tribute; causeway; quipu; road network; terrace farming
notes: Classic Maya cities (Tikal, Copan, about 250 to 900), the Mexica (Aztec) state and its capital Tenochtitlan, and the Inca state with its road network, quipu records and Cusco and Machu Picchu. Builds on grade 6's ancient Central and South America. Sources include the peoples' own (Maya glyphs, Mexica codices) as well as later Spanish accounts, which are sourced for their purpose. Present tense as well as past: millions of Maya people live in Guatemala, Mexico and Belize and speak Mayan languages; Nahuatl and Quechua are spoken by millions today, told from these communities' own published materials. Teacher note: Mexica human sacrifice is named plainly from the record, without letting it stand for the whole society. Builds on ss6-maya-andes-research (grade 6); the handoff skips 2 grades because grade 7 covers South and East Asia, Oceania and Europe and grade 8 is civics; this region's history resumes in grade 9 world history. Handoff kind: from ss6-maya-andes-research (grade 6) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by ss7-research-greek and ss8-court-research.

words: feudalism; vassal; manor; serf; chivalry; Magna Carta; Holy Roman Empire
notes: The kingdoms and feudal societies of Europe (England, France, Spain, Russia, the Holy Roman Empire): lords, vassals and serfs on the manor; knighthood and chivalry; the Church's growing wealth and its 11th century struggles with kings over who appoints bishops; and the first limits on royal power in England (Magna Carta, 1215, and early Parliament). Students compare European feudalism with Kamakura Japan using the terms from wh1-forms-of-power. Magna Carta is taught as a baron's charter whose meaning grew later. Builds on ss7-rome-fall (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-rome-fall (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: city-state; banking; merchant; patron; republic
notes: Venice, Florence and Genoa: banking and early capitalism, trade with the Byzantine and Ottoman Empires and Asia, merchant republics, and families who paid for art. The row explains why wealth from Mediterranean trade made the Renaissance possible (picked up in wh1-renaissance). Venice's and Genoa's roles in the Black Sea slave trade are named plainly.

words: enslave; war captive; bondage; slave market; hereditary
notes: How common it was, from the 400s to the 1700s, for societies across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas to enslave war captives and to buy and sell people: trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean trades, Slavic captives sold in the Mediterranean, captives in Mesoamerica. Students compare the forms (household, military, agricultural; whether status passed to children; whether people could gain freedom). The comparison sets up why the Atlantic system (wh1-atlantic-slave-trade) was different in scale and in being hereditary and tied to race. Teacher note: plain facts; the comparison must never be used to make any system seem mild; enslaved people's own words where they survive; no role play or simulation. Builds on ss7-roman-slavery-class (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-roman-slavery-class (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: al-Andalus; coexistence; crusade; pilgrimage; jihad; pogrom
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.6 (point of view in an account)
notes: Muslim and Christian kingdoms of the Mediterranean: periods of coexistence, tolerance and trade (al-Andalus, Norman Sicily) and the Crusades of the 11th to 13th centuries, their causes, course and results. Crusader, Byzantine, Muslim and Jewish accounts are read side by side, and students analyse what shaped each writer's view (faith, place, status, what they stood to gain). Includes the massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhineland in 1096 and the sack of Constantinople in 1204. Historians disagree on how tolerant al-Andalus was; the unit carries more than one account. Teacher note: religious violence named plainly on all sides; no faith today is blamed for the acts of the 1100s.

words: pandemic; bubonic plague; mortality rate; scapegoat; labor shortage
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent of a population lost)
notes: How the bubonic plague spread along Eurasian and African trade routes in the 1300s, its death rates (perhaps a third or more of Europe's people between 1347 and 1351, with heavy losses in the Middle East, North Africa and China), and its many effects: labor shortages and higher wages, revolts, religious movements, and the murder of Jewish communities blamed for the plague. Students build a multi-cause, multi-effect chain and weigh which effects lasted. Geography: a catastrophe reshapes trade, politics and migration. Teacher note: the massacres of Jews are named plainly.

words: translation; manuscript; monastery; House of Wisdom; university; scholasticism
notes: How Greek, Roman and other classical learning survived after Rome's fall in the west: Islamic scholars in Baghdad and Cordoba translating and adding to Greek and Indian works, Christian monasteries copying texts, and the rise of universities in the Islamic world and Europe from the 800s to the 1200s (al-Qarawiyyin, Bologna, Paris, Oxford). The skill is continuity and change: what carried on, what was changed by those who carried it, and how the same texts reached Europe through Arabic. Builds on ss7-ideas-spread (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-ideas-spread (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: gunpowder; compass; woodblock printing; papermaking; diffusion
notes: Gunpowder, the magnetic compass, printing and papermaking: how each spread from China across Asia, the Islamic world and Europe, and what each changed (warfare and fortification, navigation, books and literacy, record keeping). Students trace one invention's route on a map and its effects in two places.

words: irrigation; crop diffusion; surplus; textile; export; demand
cross_subject: science:HS-ESS3-1 (land and water shape farming)
notes: The medieval Agricultural Revolution in Africa, Europe and Asia (new crops such as citrus, rice, sugar and cotton spread into Spain; large irrigation works; the heavy plough and three-field rotation) and India's cotton textile economy, whose cloth was a key export to Africa and Europe. Reintroduces supply and demand for this course: why demand for Indian cloth far from India kept prices and production high, and what a surplus makes possible. Geography: how settlement and farming changed the land. Builds on ss7-silk-road-trade (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-silk-road-trade (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: Renaissance; humanism; perspective drawing; patron; vernacular
notes: The European Renaissance: its roots in Italian city-state wealth and in classical texts reaching Europe, humanism, and key Italian and Northern European artists, writers and inventors (Leonardo, Michelangelo, Christine de Pizan, Erasmus, Durer). The historical skill is significance: students ask why some figures are called significant now who were not in their own time, and others the reverse, and how the label Renaissance itself was given later.

words: Reformation; indulgence; Protestant; Counter-Reformation; Jesuit; persecution
notes: The Protestant Reformation (discontent with the Church, Luther and Calvin, the printing press, the Church of England), the Catholic Counter-Reformation (the Council of Trent, Ignatius Loyola and the Jesuits), and how both shifted power in Europe, led to persecution of religious minorities (Anabaptists, Jews, Catholics or Protestants where they were the minority) and fed wars. Pamphlets and woodcuts from both sides are read as persuasion. Luther's writings against Jews are named plainly. Teacher note: describe each faith's beliefs as its followers do; no side is the hero. Builds on ss6-christianity-origins (grade 6); the handoff skips 2 grades because grade 7 covers South and East Asia, Oceania and Europe and grade 8 is civics; this region's history resumes in grade 9 world history. Handoff kind: from ss6-christianity-origins (grade 6) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: middle class; joint-stock company; stock exchange; global trade; Golden Age
notes: The rise of a wealthy Protestant middle class in 17th century Northern Europe, especially the Dutch Republic: chartered trading companies and the joint-stock form, the Amsterdam exchange, global trade, and money spent on art and science (Rembrandt, Vermeer, the microscope). The same trade included the conquest of the Banda Islands in the 1620s and Dutch slave trading, named plainly. Students explain how shared investment spread risk and why that changed trade. Builds on ss7-silk-road-trade (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Handoff kind: from ss7-silk-road-trade (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: scientific method; hypothesis; heliocentric; telescope; microscope; navigation
cross_subject: science:HS-ESS1-4 (models of orbital motion)
notes: How the scientific method and new tools (telescope, microscope) produced new theories of the universe; two figures studied closely (for example Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton, or Maria Sibylla Merian); and how better ships, maps and instruments made European voyages possible. Includes Islamic and Chinese astronomy that came before. Students explain a change in explanation (earth-centred to sun-centred) from evidence, not as a single genius moment.

words: expulsion; Inquisition; conquistador; sea route; spice trade
notes: Why Europeans wanted a sea route to Asia (the spice trade, Ottoman and Venetian control of routes, rival monarchies), and Spain and Portugal after 1492: the expulsion of Jews and later Muslims, the Spanish Inquisition, and expeditions to conquer and convert the Americas and the Philippines. Teacher note: expulsion and forced conversion named plainly, with the communities' own later records (Sephardic and Morisco).

words: Columbian Exchange; epidemic; encomienda; mission; colony; plantation
notes: The effects of European colonization in the Americas and Caribbean: the Columbian Exchange of crops, animals and diseases in both directions; the collapse of Native populations by up to 90 percent in many regions within about a century, from epidemics, war and forced labor (encomienda, mita); missionaries and their effects; and the growth of the transatlantic slave trade to work plantations and mines (carried in wh1-atlantic-slave-trade). Geography: how new crops and animals changed land use and trade on both sides of the ocean. Present tense: the Taino people's descendants and their organizations in the Caribbean and the United States today, and the Native nations of Mexico and the Andes, from their own published materials. Teacher note: conquest and epidemic named plainly; Native people shown resisting and adapting, not only dying. Builds on ss6-caribbean-peoples (grade 6); the handoff skips 2 grades because grade 7 covers South and East Asia, Oceania and Europe and grade 8 is civics; this region's history resumes in grade 9 world history. Handoff kind: from ss6-caribbean-peoples (grade 6) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: transatlantic slave trade; Middle Passage; chattel slavery; plantation; resistance; abolition
cross_subject: math:6.RP.A.3c (percent of people who died in the crossing)
notes: Carries the transatlantic slave trade part of MA.WHI.T5.3 (named on wh1-colonial-americas). About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships from the 1500s to the 1860s and about 10.7 million survived the crossing; the trade's routes, the African states and European traders involved, the Middle Passage, plantation slavery in Brazil and the Caribbean, and slavery made hereditary and tied to race. Resistance on ships and plantations, maroon communities, and lives and cultures built. The source skill (D2.His.8): most records were made by traders and owners, so students ask what the surviving records can and cannot show, and use the few accounts by enslaved people (Equiano) with care. Teacher note: plain facts; no role play or simulation of the crossing or of sale; enslaved people's own words where they exist. Builds on ss5-slavery-colonies (grade 5); the handoff skips 3 grades because grades 6 to 8 (ancient world and civics) do not return to Atlantic slavery. MA.WHI.T5.3 is shared with the row that owns it; this row teaches the Atlantic slave trade part of it (its scale, routes and effects), while that row keeps the rest. Students also test one current interpretation (how much the trade shaped West African states) against the record they have studied. Handoff kind: from ss5-slavery-colonies (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: empire; trading post; colony; diplomacy; envoy
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.8 (gathering information from sources)
notes: Map the 17th century Ottoman, Chinese (Ming and Qing), Portuguese, Dutch, Spanish and British empires and explain how location shaped their politics and trade (sea empires of ports and trading posts, land empires of provinces). Students then report on one first-hand account of travel, trade or diplomacy from that century (for example a Jesuit in Beijing, an Ottoman traveller such as Evliya Celebi, an English envoy to the Mughal court), sourced for its writer's purpose. Builds on ss7-europe-geo (grade 7); the handoff skips a grade because grade 8 is a civics year; world history resumes in grade 9. Map scale and latitude-longitude from grades 4 to 7 open with a short retrieval task. Handoff kind: from ss7-europe-geo (grade 7) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: Enlightenment; reason; natural rights; social contract; separation of powers; salon
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (evaluating an argument)
notes: The origins and ideals of the European Enlightenment (reason, progress, liberty, natural rights) and how thinkers such as Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Voltaire and Mary Wollstonecraft challenged existing power. Students read short excerpts and state each argument, and note whom it left out (many Enlightenment writers defended slavery or excluded women, and others attacked both).

words: Mandate of Heaven; absolute monarchy; enlightened absolutism; constitutional monarchy; divine right
notes: Historical philosophies of government with world examples: the Chinese Mandate of Heaven (a ruler must be worthy), absolute monarchy (Louis XIV), enlightened absolutism (Peter the Great, Catherine the Great), and constitutional monarchy (English tradition from Magna Carta). Students evaluate each system by what it promised and how it treated its people, and compare where each placed the source of legitimate power. Builds on grade 8's philosophical foundations of government and wh1-forms-of-power.

words: Parliament; civil war; Glorious Revolution; Bill of Rights; consent
notes: Why England became the exception to the growth of absolutism: the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, the Commonwealth, the Restoration and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 (T6.3a), and the English Bill of Rights of 1689 limiting the monarch without Parliament's consent (T6.3b). Students build the cause chain and explain how Parliament's control of taxes was the hinge.

words: constitutional democracy; republic; Bill of Rights; ratify; amendment
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.9 (seminal US founding documents)
notes: How constitutional democracy developed after the American Revolution, through the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, seen from world history: what the founders took from English and Enlightenment ideas, what was new (a written constitution, federalism, an amendment process), and who was left out in 1787 (enslaved people, women, Native nations). Grade 8 civics taught the structure; grade 9 places it in the world story the next year carries into the French and Haitian revolutions. Kept short.

words: interpretation; secondary source; historian; corroborate; follow-up question
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.6 (author purpose and point of view)
notes: How a historian's account (a secondary interpretation) is built from primary sources: students trace a claim in a textbook passage back to the sources behind it, and use questions raised by several sources to find further ones. Example: two historians' accounts of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage and the Arabic sources they each rely on. Grows the grade 6 to 8 primary and secondary distinction into seeing the link between them; grade 10 critiques interpretations (wh2-historians-interpretations).

words: claim; counterclaim; evidence; reasoning; thesis; rebuttal
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.1 (argument with claims and counterclaims); ela:W.9-10.2 (explanatory writing)
notes: Write a sourced argument and a sourced explanation: a precise claim, evidence drawn from several named sources, reasoning that says why the evidence supports the claim, a counterclaim stated fairly and answered, and the limits of the evidence named. Students revise a claim when sources disagree. Grows from short paragraphs in the first unit to a multi-page argument by the end of grade 9; grade 10 adds critique of others' arguments and a research paper (wh2-research-argument). World History I's yearly action cycle: students find one public telling of world history near them (a museum label, a monument plaque, a local web page or a textbook passage), check it against the evidence, and if they find it wrong or incomplete, choose whether to write a proposed correction to its keeper through the school. Action is the student's choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks.

words: interpretation; contested; historiography; disciplinary concept
notes: Build questions where experts disagree: students name what historians or economists agree and disagree on about a compelling question (Did the Treaty of Versailles cause the Second World War? Was decolonization won or granted?) and which concepts in a supporting question are open to interpretation (nation, revolution, success). Grade 9 framed and planned an inquiry; grade 10 builds it around a live disagreement among scholars. The same check is applied to each supporting question, not only the compelling one.

words: sovereignty; nation state; Peace of Westphalia; Versailles; serfdom; Westernization
notes: The growing concentration of power in European states from 1500 to 1800: the Thirty Years War and the Peace of Westphalia as the start of the sovereign state system, Louis XIV and Versailles, Russian czars and Peter the Great's Westernization with serfdom spreading, and the rise of Prussia, Poland and Sweden. MA.WHII.T1.2 (the Glorious Revolution and England as the exception) repeats grade 9's MA.WHI.T6.3: here it is a short recall used as the contrast case, not retaught.

words: Estates-General; Third Estate; Declaration of the Rights of Man; Reign of Terror; Napoleon
notes: The political, social, intellectual and economic causes of the French Revolution (Enlightenment ideas, debt, a rising middle class, a failing monarchy, bread prices) and its main events from 1789 through the Terror to Napoleon. Students judge whether it met its own stated goals of liberty, equality and fraternity, for whom, and by when, including Olympe de Gouges's claim for women. Teacher note: the Terror's executions named plainly.

words: revolution; Haitian Revolution; abolition; self-emancipation; independence
notes: Compare the causes, goals and outcomes of the American, French and Haitian Revolutions and their short and long term effects on world history. The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) is taught as what it was: enslaved people freeing themselves and founding the first state to end slavery permanently, led by Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, followed by the indemnity France forced Haiti to pay from 1825. Students write a comparison argument from sources of all three. Teacher note: plain facts about slavery and its violence; no role play.

words: nationalism; unification; realpolitik; balance of power; Kaiser
notes: Italian and German unification: causes (nationalism, language, economics, war), methods (Cavour's diplomacy, Garibaldi, Bismarck's wars), and the effect on Europe's balance of power, which grade 10 returns to in the causes of the First World War. Students compare two paths to a nation state on maps of before and after.

words: independence; creole; caudillo; abolition; hacienda; Indigenous
notes: Political, social and economic change in 19th century Mexico, Central America and South America: wars of independence (Hidalgo and Morelos, Bolivar, San Martin), rule by strongmen, the end of slavery (Brazil last, in 1888), economies built on exports, and the place of Indigenous peoples, compared with Europe in the same century. Present tense: Indigenous nations of Mexico and the Andes today, and their own accounts of the 19th century, from their own published materials.

words: Industrial Revolution; enclosure; steam engine; factory system; capital; industrialization
cross_subject: science:HS-PS3-3 (machines that convert energy)
notes: The economic, political, social and technological factors behind the Agricultural and Industrial Revolutions in Britain (enclosure and new farming, coal, capital, colonial markets and raw cotton grown by enslaved people in the Americas, inventions such as the steam engine), and how industry spread to Europe and the United States and shifted the balance of power. Students build a cause chain that weighs these factors against each other.

words: urbanization; tenement; child labor; pollution; inequality; working class
cross_subject: science:HS-ESS3-4 (reducing human impact on the environment); math:8.F.B.5 (reading a graph of change over time)
notes: The economic and social effects of industrialization in England: migration to cities, a growing middle class, wealth inequality, pollution, and hard, dangerous work for the urban poor and for children. Students read population and wage data alongside factory inspectors' reports and workers' testimony, and explain how economic choices reshaped cities and the countryside.

words: socialism; communism; feminism; labor union; reform; suffrage
notes: New philosophies the Industrial Revolution produced, read from short excerpts: early feminism, socialism (Robert Owen), communism (Marx and Engels), and liberal and conservative replies; then British reform movements (labor unions, factory acts, the widening of the vote, Chartists and later women's suffrage) and the laws they won. Students explain each idea as its supporters did and as its critics did, before judging it.

words: imperialism; colony; protectorate; Berlin Conference; raw material; capital
cross_subject: math:6.SP.B.5 (summarizing data in context)
notes: Map the places outside Europe that European states controlled in the 19th century (British India, French and British Africa, Portuguese Brazil until 1822, Spanish colonies) at world and regional scale, and explain the causes of 19th century imperialism: centuries of rivalry for wealth, resources and strategic advantage (T3.2a), and the capital that slavery and the slave trade generated for industrializing Europe (T3.2b, taught with the historians' debate over how large that share was). Students use maps and data at more than one scale to explain the pattern.

words: colonialism; resistance; Opium War; Raj; partition; forced labor
notes: The impact of Western imperialism in Asia (British rule in India and the 1857 rising, the Opium Wars in China, Japan's own empire), Africa (the scramble and the Berlin Conference, the Congo Free State's forced labor and mutilation, the Herero and Nama genocide, Ethiopia's victory at Adwa in 1896) and Latin America (economic dependence). Students analyse how the context of empire shaped how colonizers and colonized saw each other then, and how it shapes views in those nations today. Teacher note: atrocities named plainly; colonized peoples shown resisting and governing, not only suffering; no images of mutilation used.

words: exoticism; anthropology; exposition; impressionism; colonial literature
cross_subject: ela:RL.9-10.6 (a cultural experience in literature from outside the United States)
notes: How colonial encounters and trade changed Western culture: export porcelain and cloth, new foods, the new fields of archaeology and anthropology, world's fairs and museums showing objects and at times people, Japanese and African art in impressionism and cubism, and colonialism in the writing of Kipling, Conrad, Stevenson, Morel and Dinesen. The skill (D2.His.6): how the views of those who wrote about empire shaped the history and the images that came down to us. Students read one short colonial text and one response from a colonized writer. Teacher note: period texts can hold slurs; the excerpt avoids printing them (rule 6).

words: militarism; alliance; imperialism; nationalism; assassination; long-term cause; trigger
notes: The causes of the First World War: Germany's rise, nationalism, imperial rivalry, militarism and the alliance system, and the assassination at Sarajevo in 1914. The skill is telling long-term causes from the triggering event in a historical argument. The skill of weighing several causes against each other comes from grade 9's Black Death (wh1-black-death); Britain's place in the alliance system is taught here in grade 10. Students rank causes and defend the ranking from sources.

words: total war; trench warfare; conscription; propaganda; rationing; armistice
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (describing a graph of production over time)
notes: The First World War as total war: industrial weapons and trench warfare and the huge casualties (T4.2a); the war's spread worldwide, with soldiers and laborers from India, Africa, China and elsewhere, and why the United States entered (T4.2b); and the home fronts, with conscription, propaganda, rationing and state control of industry (T4.2c). Propaganda posters from several countries are sourced as persuasion. Teacher note: casualty facts plain; no graphic images chosen for shock. Students read a chart of one country's war production over the years and describe how fast it grew and when.

standard: MA.WHII.T4.3; MA.WHII.T4.3a; MA.WHII.T4.3b; MA.WHII.T4.3c; MA.WHII.T4.3d; MA.WHII.T4.3e; MA.WHII.T4.3g; MA.WHII.T4.3h; MA.WHII.T4.3i; MA.WHII.T4.4; D2.Civ.3.9-12; D2.Geo.5.9-12
words: Treaty of Versailles; reparations; mandate; League of Nations; modernism; pandemic
notes: What followed the First World War: economic ruin, the Lost Generation, the fall of the Russian, Ottoman and Austrian empires, Ataturk's Turkey, the mandates and new borders of the Middle East, the Paris Peace Conference and Versailles, the 1918 to 1920 influenza pandemic, and modernism in the arts. The Armenian genocide (T4.3f) has its own row (wh2-armenian-genocide). Students evaluate whether Versailles addressed the war's problems, and explain how decisions made in Paris drew borders that still shape the region (before and after maps). Civics: how treaties and the League tried and failed to keep order. Students also trace effects beyond the borders drawn (refugees moving, trade routes cut, later conflicts in neighbouring lands).

words: genocide; deportation; death march; denial; testimony
notes: The Armenian genocide of 1915 to 1923: the Ottoman government's deportation and mass killing of Armenians (about a million or more dead), with Assyrians and Greeks also targeted. Taught as genocide, which is the finding of the historians and scholars of genocide who study it (values rule b), with the Turkish state's denial named as denial and studied as a case of how a past is contested. Survivors' testimony, diplomats' reports and photographs are sourced and corroborated. Armenian communities today in Armenia and the diaspora, from their own published materials. Teacher note: plain facts, no graphic images chosen for shock, no role play.

words: czar; Bolshevik; soviet; civil war; New Economic Policy; USSR
notes: Russia from the unrest under Nicholas II through the two revolutions of 1917, the Bolshevik seizure of power and the Russian Civil War, in the context of the First World War; then the creation of the USSR, the New Economic Policy, early cultural experiment, Lenin's death and the struggle that put Stalin in power. Students build a timeline of 1905 to 1928 and explain at which points another outcome was possible.

words: depression; unemployment; inflation; monetary policy; tariff; Keynesian
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (describing a graph of unemployment over time); math:7.RP.A.3 (percent change)
notes: The causes and consequences of the global economic collapse of the 1930s and how governments responded: tight money and the gold standard (T4.7a), unemployment and inflation, including German hyperinflation earlier (T4.7b), political instability in weak democracies such as Germany (T4.7c), and the competing economic ideas of Keynes, von Mises, Hayek and Friedman (T4.7d). Students read unemployment and price data and explain each school's account of what went wrong and what to do, before evaluating one government's response. The economics course later takes the models further.

words: fascism; totalitarianism; dictator; propaganda; purge; collectivization
notes: The features of fascism and totalitarianism in Mussolini's Italy, Hitler's Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union, and the conditions that let each rise (war, depression, fear, weak institutions); how each repressed dissent and persecuted minorities: the Nazi laws against Jews, Stalin's purges, the Gulag, and the famine of 1932 to 1933 that killed millions in Ukraine (the Holodomor) and Kazakhstan. Propaganda is sourced as propaganda. Teacher note: plain facts; the regimes' own words appear only as sources to be analysed.

words: aggression; appeasement; League of Nations; annexation; Nazi-Soviet Pact
notes: The aggression of Germany, Italy and Japan in the 1930s and early 1940s and the weak response of the League and the Western democracies: Italy's invasion of Ethiopia (T4.10a), the Spanish Civil War (T4.10b), Japan's invasion of Manchuria and China, including the Nanjing Massacre, and of the Philippines (T4.10c), and German moves into the Rhineland, Austria, Czechoslovakia and Poland with the Nazi-Soviet Pact (T4.10d). Students map the steps on a timeline and judge appeasement with what leaders knew at the time. Teacher note: the Nanjing Massacre named plainly, including its denial.

words: Allies; Axis; turning point; Big Three; Yalta; Potsdam
notes: One battle studied in depth for how it changed the war's course and the countries involved (Britain, Midway, Stalingrad, Normandy or Iwo Jima: students choose, the class hears several), and the goals, strategies and postwar plans of Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Stalin, through the wartime conferences that shaped the war's end and the start of the Cold War. No battle role play or war game that puts students in combat roles.

words: Holocaust; antisemitism; dehumanization; ghetto; concentration camp; genocide; rescuer
notes: The Holocaust: its roots in centuries of Christian antisemitism and 19th century ideas of race and nation; Nazi dehumanization, laws, ghettos, mass shootings and death camps; the planned murder of about six million Jews; and the persecution and murder of Roma people, disabled people, gay men and others. Jewish life before the war, resistance (the Warsaw Ghetto uprising), rescuers, bystanders and perpetrators. Survivors' testimony is read and sourced. Teacher note: no simulations, role play or 'what would you do' games; no images chosen for shock; denial is named as false and not debated as a view.

words: atomic bomb; Hiroshima; Nagasaki; surrender; deterrence; hibakusha
cross_subject: science:HS-PS1-8 (energy released in nuclear fission)
notes: The United States' decision to use atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945: the reasons given (ending the war quickly, avoiding an invasion), the death toll (well over 100,000 by the end of 1945), the survivors' (hibakusha) accounts, and the effect on relations with the Soviet Union. The skill (D2.His.7): how views in the present, in the United States, Japan and elsewhere, shape how the decision is interpreted. Students weigh the evidence used for each interpretation. Teacher note: more than one view is taught; casualties named plainly.

words: superpower; United Nations; Universal Declaration of Human Rights; Nuremberg; Geneva Conventions; decolonization
notes: The global consequences of the Second World War: the destruction of bombed cities, about 70 to 85 million dead and tens of millions displaced, European support for reform and decolonization, the United States and Soviet Union as superpowers, the nuclear arms race, and new international law: the United Nations, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Nuremberg tribunal and principles, and the expanded Geneva Conventions. Civics: how human rights became a shared standard and how far personal and national interests shape how states apply it.

words: Cold War; capitalism; communism; Iron Curtain; NATO; Warsaw Pact; non-aligned
notes: The contrasting worldviews of the United States and the Soviet Union and how their rivalry split Europe into East and West; how the UN, NATO, the Warsaw Pact and the non-aligned movement (India, Egypt, Indonesia, Yugoslavia) shaped the Cold War. Students map the blocs and read each side's own statements as sources.

words: containment; Berlin airlift; Berlin Wall; uprising; arms control; detente
notes: Cold War developments centred on Europe and the arms race: the division of Germany and the Berlin crises of 1948 and 1961 (T5.3a), Soviet life after Stalin and the risings in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968 (T5.3c), the arms race and treaties such as ABM and SALT (T5.3g), and detente (T5.3h). The standard asks students to evaluate how one development affected how the Cold War turned out: each student takes one case from this row or wh2-cold-war-world in depth, and the class compares.

words: Marshall Plan; proxy war; coup; Korean War; Vietnam War; Cuban Missile Crisis
notes: The Cold War beyond Europe: the Marshall Plan, containment in the Korean and Vietnam Wars and China's rise (T5.3b); the United States' backing of the overthrow of governments in Iran in 1953 and Guatemala in 1954 (T5.3d); rivalry in the Middle East and the Soviet war in Afghanistan (T5.3e); the Cuban Revolution and the Missile Crisis (T5.3f). Told with the people of each country as actors, not only as a board for the superpowers. Teacher note: civilian deaths in these wars named plainly; Guatemala's later civil war atrocities connect to wh2-genocide-atrocity.

words: Communist Party; Great Leap Forward; famine; Cultural Revolution; Tiananmen; reform
notes: China after 1945: the civil war and Communist victory in 1949, Mao's Great Leap Forward and the famine that followed (tens of millions dead; estimates vary), the Cultural Revolution, Deng Xiaoping's market reforms, and the 1989 Tiananmen protests and their crushing. Students compare official Chinese accounts with other records and survivors' memoirs, sourcing each. Teacher note: facts plain; the Chinese people are separated from the state's decisions.

words: decolonization; nationalism; independence; nonviolent resistance; partition; liberation movement
notes: The goals of nationalist movements across Asia, Africa and the Middle East after 1945 and how one movement and its leader won independence, studied in depth (for example India with Gandhi, the partition of 1947 and its mass violence and displacement; Ghana with Nkrumah; Kenya, including the British camps of the Mau Mau years; Algeria; Vietnam). The civics skill: compare the means people used to change their societies (nonviolence, negotiation, armed struggle, international pressure) and what each cost. Teacher note: partition violence and colonial repression named plainly. Students then set those means beside ones used today (consumer boycotts, online organizing, international courts, truth commissions) and say which earlier means are still used and what is new.

words: apartheid; segregation; pass laws; African National Congress; sanctions; Truth and Reconciliation
notes: How apartheid in South Africa (1948 to 1991) was defended by its government and resisted by South Africans: pass laws, forced removals, Sharpeville and Soweto, the African National Congress, Nelson Mandela's imprisonment, international sanctions and the role of the UN, and the negotiated end. Students read the government's own arguments as sources and set them against resisters' words. Teacher note: plain facts about violence; no role play of segregation.

words: Zionism; Mandate Palestine; partition plan; Nakba; refugee; two-state solution
notes: The background to Israel's founding in 1948 and the wars and conflicts that followed: Zionism and Jewish immigration from Eastern Europe (T5.7a); antisemitism and the Holocaust as background (T5.7b); the 1947 UN partition vote (T5.7c); the war of 1948, which Israelis call the War of Independence and Palestinians call the Nakba, in which about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled and lost their land (T5.7d), and the Arab states' rejection of partition and invasion (T5.7e); the wars since, including 1967 and 1973 (T5.7f); the region's many peoples and faiths today (T5.7g); and peace efforts, including the two-state proposal (T5.7h). Both peoples are present tense, from their own published materials, with the record deciding facts. Teacher note: a sensitive, living topic for many families; every contested event carries more than one account, maps are dated and sourced, and Jewish refugees from Arab countries after 1948 are named too.

words: glasnost; perestroika; Solidarity; revolution of 1989; oligarch; proliferation
notes: Why the Soviet Union and the communist governments of Eastern Europe declined and fell (the costly arms race, weak economies, the Afghan war, Solidarity in Poland, lost public support, Gorbachev's reforms, 1989 and 1991), and the effects of the breakup: the turn to market economies, instability, the danger of loose nuclear material, and the rise of oligarchic power into the 21st century. Students weigh internal against external causes. A planned economy's shortages (empty shelves, long lines while prices were fixed) are named as one internal cause.

words: productivity; standard of living; guest worker; economic integration; European Community
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (comparing growth on a graph)
notes: What drove the postwar rise in productivity and living standards in Western Europe and Japan: lasting peace, Marshall aid, migrant and guest workers (from Turkey, North Africa, the Caribbean, South Asia), and international bodies such as the European Coal and Steel Community and the trade agreements that followed. Students read growth data and explain which factors mattered most, and whose labor built the growth.

words: relativity; quantum; radioactivity; vaccine; DNA; integrated circuit; internet
cross_subject: science:HS-LS1-1 (DNA structure and proteins); science:HS-PS1-8 (radioactivity and nuclear processes)
notes: How 20th century science changed what people know about nature, their daily lives and later research, studied through one case in depth (Einstein, Bohr, the Curies, Fermi and Oppenheimer, von Braun, Salk, the discovery of DNA's structure including Rosalind Franklin's work, the integrated circuit, the early networks that became the internet, Sylvia Earle, Jane Goodall), with the class hearing several. Hard questions stay in: von Braun's Nazi past and the forced labor that built his rockets, and the ethics of the atomic bomb.

words: feminism; LGBTQ rights; environmentalism; civil rights; social movement
notes: How late 20th century social and intellectual movements (feminism, LGBTQ rights, environmentalism, movements for racial equality) changed assumptions about race, class, gender, religion and nature, across several countries. Students trace what changed, for whom, and what stayed, using movement documents and opponents' arguments as sources. Teacher note (values rule c and d): LGBTQ people appear here as the history includes them, plainly and with dignity; content suits grade 10; families' differing views are respected and students are not asked to state their own.

words: globalization; outsourcing; supply chain; free trade; developing country; tariff
cross_subject: math:8.F.B.5 (reading trade and wage data over time)
notes: Why globalization grew after 1991 (trade agreements, container shipping, the internet, China's opening) and its effects on workers in richer and poorer countries: factory jobs lost and gained, wages, prices, the environment and rights at work. Geography: how competition for scarce resources brings both cooperation and conflict between countries. Students weigh evidence on both sides. The economics course (grades 11 to 12) takes trade theory further; this row is the history and its effects.

words: Islamism; Iranian Revolution; Gulf War; Arab Spring; ISIS; sectarian
notes: Major forces in the Middle East since 1980: the Iranian Revolution, rivalry between Saudi Arabia and Iran, Islamist movements, the Iran-Iraq War, the Gulf and Iraq wars, the Arab uprisings of 2011 and the wars in Syria and Yemen, and ISIS. Students map the region and explain one development from sources from inside it. Teacher note: Islamism as a political movement is kept distinct from Islam as a faith practised by most Muslims, who reject violence; civilian suffering named plainly.

words: populism; party platform; election; superpower; Belt and Road; South China Sea
notes: Two changes in 21st century power: populist movements and parties in Europe and their strength (from election results and the parties' own platforms), and China's growing economic and political power and role in the world. Students describe each from its own statements and from data before evaluating. Teacher note (values rule b): no party or country today is labelled good or bad; claims are decided by evidence; current events are dated, as they will change.

words: climate change; humanitarian; refugee; child mortality; sustainable; informed action
cross_subject: science:HS-ESS3-5 (climate data and forecasts)
notes: How well international efforts have met global problems: climate change, habitat protection and farm output (T6.5a), and AIDS and other disease, child mortality, refugee crises, education for girls and women, and rural economies (T6.5b). Geography: how climate change shapes migration, settlement and land use. Students use more than one discipline to explain a problem, weigh the evidence on what has worked, and assess options for action. This is the course's informed action: each student chooses whether and how to act, informed by evidence; the course picks no cause. Builds on ss8-civic-action (grade 8); World History I's action cycle (wh1-historical-argument) comes between. Handoff kind: from ss8-civic-action (grade 8) is a maintained skill, kept in use between by wh1-historical-argument.

words: genocide; mass atrocity; ethnic cleansing; Genocide Convention; tribunal; prevention
notes: Tell genocide (the 1948 Genocide Convention's legal definition) from other mass atrocity, and analyse the causes in one modern case studied in depth: Northern Ireland, Bosnia and Kosovo, Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge, Rwanda and the Congo, Darfur and South Sudan, Kashmir, Sri Lanka, Guatemala and Syria, Shi'a and Sunni conflict, or the Rohingya in Myanmar. The class meets several cases briefly and finds common causes and warning signs, and how courts and states have responded. Teacher note: survivors' testimony with care; no graphic images chosen for shock; no role play; students who may have family ties to a case are given a choice of case.

words: terrorism; Al-Qaeda; Taliban; ISIS; counterterrorism; civil liberties
notes: The people, events and conditions behind international terrorism, including Al-Qaeda and the attacks of September 11, 2001, the Taliban and ISIS, and how governments and societies have responded (wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, security laws, debates over civil liberties). Students evaluate one response from evidence. Teacher note: no group or faith is blamed for the acts of a few; victims named with dignity; images of the attacks used sparingly.

words: historiography; interpretation; bias; limitation; credibility; peer review
cross_subject: ela:RI.9-10.8 (judging the reasoning and evidence of a text)
notes: Critique secondary history: detect the limits of a kind of evidence and of competing interpretations, judge whether a historian's sources fit the claim made, check a source's credibility by how experts in the field rate it, and critique a work of history in print, film or a museum display for accuracy. Example: two interpretations of the Treaty of Versailles or of the causes of decolonization. Grade 9 traced interpretations back to sources; grade 10 judges them.

words: research paper; thesis; synthesis; citation; audience; peer critique
cross_subject: ela:W.9-10.1 (written argument); ela:W.9-10.7 (sustained research); ela:SL.9-10.4 (presenting to an audience)
notes: Integrate evidence from many primary sources and interpretations into a reasoned research argument on a modern world history question, then critique classmates' claims, evidence and reasoning and revise. Students adapt the argument for an audience beyond the classroom (a short talk, a letter, a museum-style panel, a map). Grade 9 wrote sourced arguments from given sets; grade 10 finds its own sources and answers critique. Hands the full research argument to the US history courses. Critique covers explanations too: students judge whether another student's explanation names enough causes and links them.

words: compelling question; supporting question; enduring issue; credibility; provenance; historiography
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.7 (short and sustained research projects); ela:W.11-12.8 (gather and assess sources)
notes: The high school research cycle, taught in full on the first US History I research task and used all year: write a compelling question that names an enduring issue (who counts as a citizen, how far federal power reaches), break it into supporting questions, and say where historians agree and disagree about it. Choose sources on purpose: a range of views, kinds of source and makers; judge a source by its maker, date, place, audience and purpose, and by how experts in the field rate it. Grade 11 depth: students build their own question and source set, where earlier grades worked from a question and set the teacher gave. Students use all five checks from grade 9 (origin, authority, structure, context, corroborative value) on each source.

words: Seven Years' War; Proclamation of 1763; Parliament; representation; boycott; Sons of Liberty; sovereignty
notes: Why the colonies broke with Britain, 1754 to 1775: the French and Indian War inside the global Seven Years' War and its debt; the Proclamation Line, the Stamp, Tea and Intolerable Acts; Patriot answers (boycotts, the Sons of Liberty, the Boston Tea Party) and the Boston and Massachusetts people at the center. Each act is read three ways: as Parliament saw it, as colonists saw it, and as Native nations saw it (Pontiac's War of 1763, led by the Odawa leader Pontiac, came before the Proclamation). The skill: sort economic, intellectual and cultural causes and weigh them, not list them. The Odawa and other Great Lakes nations govern themselves today. Builds on ss5-revolution-causes (grade 5); the handoff skips 5 grades because grades 6 to 10 are world history and civics; US history before 1920 returns in grade 11 US History I. Handoff kind: from ss5-revolution-causes (grade 5) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: natural rights; unalienable; consent of the governed; grievance; equality; rule of law
cross_subject: ela:RI.11-12.9 (founding documents read for their themes and purposes)
notes: The Declaration of Independence read as an argument: its claim (a government that breaks the people's trust may be replaced), its evidence (the list of grievances) and its reasoning from natural rights and consent. Students test the claim of equality against 1776: slavery legal in every colony, women without a vote, and a grievance that calls Native peoples savages. Teacher note: the phrase about Native peoples is discussed as the writers' view, with Native nations' own answer to it; read in full, not hidden. Later readers (Douglass in 1852, Seneca Falls in 1848) turned the same words into claims for their own rights. Builds on ss8-declaration (grade 8); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 9 and 10 are world history; US history resumes in grade 11 US History I. Builds on wh1-enlightenment (grade 9); the handoff skips a grade because grade 10 is world history since 1800; US history resumes in grade 11. Handoff kind: from ss8-declaration (grade 8) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task; from wh1-enlightenment (grade 9) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: Continental Army; militia; Loyalist; alliance; encampment; turning point
notes: The war from Lexington and Concord to Yorktown, mapped and dated: Saratoga as the turning point that brought the French alliance; Valley Forge; Washington, Greene and other leaders. The war's many participants: Loyalists; Black soldiers on both sides (the 1st Rhode Island Regiment; Dunmore's 1775 offer of freedom to men who fled to the British); women in the camps; the Haudenosaunee Confederacy split, the Oneida and Tuscarora mostly with the Patriots and most other nations with Britain, and the 1779 Sullivan campaign that burned Haudenosaunee towns. The skill: how a person's significance (Deborah Sampson, James Armistead Lafayette) is judged differently over time. The Haudenosaunee nations govern today. Builds on wh1-renaissance (grade 9); the handoff skips a grade because grade 10 is world history since 1800; US history resumes in grade 11. Handoff kind: from wh1-renaissance (grade 9) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of wh1-renaissance. The link from wh1-renaissance is a skill link (weighing how new ideas spread and took hold), so the reteach is a worked example of that skill.

words: Articles of Confederation; Shays' Rebellion; compromise; ratification; three-fifths clause; federalism
notes: From the Articles (1781) to the Constitution: why a weak central government was chosen, what it could not do, and how Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts pushed the call for a convention. The Convention's fights and deals: representation (the Great Compromise), slavery (the three-fifths clause, the 1808 slave trade clause, the fugitive slave clause), the executive and ratification. Figures in their time and place (Madison, Hamilton, Franklin, Washington). The skill: judge a decision against its moment and the options on the table, without excusing what it did. Teacher note: the slavery compromises are named plainly as protections of slavery. Builds on ss8-articles-convention (grade 8) and ss8-ratification-debate (grade 8); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 9 and 10 are world history; US history resumes in grade 11 US History I. Builds on wh1-constitutional-democracy (grade 9); the handoff skips a grade because grade 10 is world history since 1800; US history resumes in grade 11. The branches card returns with a short retrieval task before the founding debates. Handoff kind: from ss8-articles-convention (grade 8) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task; from ss8-ratification-debate (grade 8) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task; from wh1-constitutional-democracy (grade 9) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: printing press; pamphlet; partisan press; telegraph; Black press; circulation
notes: News/media literacy, placed in US History I. How news spread from the printing press to the telegraph and, in outline, radio, television and the internet, on a timeline. One case study: newspapers and pamphlets in the Revolution and the ratification debate (the Federalist essays first ran in New York newspapers), or the Black press (Freedom's Journal in 1827, Douglass's North Star in 1847). Each paper is sourced: who owned it, who read it, what it wanted. Hands on the history of the press that US Government builds on when it turns to press freedom. Builds on ss8-press-freedom (grade 8); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 9 and 10 are world history; US history resumes in grade 11 US History I. Handoff kind: from ss8-press-freedom (grade 8) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: Federalist; Democratic-Republican; political party; judicial review; neutrality; Alien and Sedition Acts
notes: Washington, Adams and Jefferson: Hamilton's financial plan and the first two parties; neutrality and the Jay Treaty; the Alien and Sedition Acts and the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions; the 1800 election as the first peaceful handover between parties; Marbury v. Madison (1803) and judicial review; the Louisiana Purchase and the embargo. The skill: evaluate each policy's effect on federal power and foreign policy with evidence, and see how party conflict started. Builds on ss8-courts-review (grade 8); the handoff skips 2 grades because grades 9 and 10 are world history; US history resumes in grade 11 US History I. Price elasticity of demand and supply computed from percent changes and used to predict how quantity responds to a price change. Builds on econ-markets-prices in the same course.

words: price ceiling; price floor; shortage; surplus; rent control; minimum wage; marginal cost; marginal benefit
cross_subject: math:A-REI.D.11 (where two graphs cross)
notes: Price and wage controls on the supply and demand graph: a ceiling (rent control) and a floor (minimum wage), with the shortages and surpluses they create and their intended and unintended results. Students build an argument with marginal benefits and marginal costs. Where economists' studies disagree (the size of minimum wage effects on jobs), both lines of evidence are taught; the student's judgment is their own. Builds on econ-markets-prices in the same course. Marginal benefit (what one more unit is worth to the buyer) and marginal cost (what one more unit costs to make) are defined before the argument uses them.

words: entrepreneur; profit; sole proprietorship; partnership; corporation; stock; bond; nonprofit
notes: Profit as the reward for the risk of failure; sole proprietorships, partnerships and corporations compared (liability, control, raising money); how firms finance themselves (retained earnings, stock, borrowing) and the trade-offs; the roles of labor unions and nonprofits in a market economy. Builds on the grade 11 rise of the corporation. Open to grade 11 or 12 (Cory, 2026-11-13): this row does not require US History I. The example it once took from us1-industrialization is retaught here in brief, from the source, so a student who has not had that course is not lost.

standard: MA.ECON.T3.4; MA.ECON.T3.5; MA.ECON.T3.6; MA.ECON.T3.7; D2.Eco.4.9-12; D2.Eco.5.9-12
words: monopoly; oligopoly; perfect competition; market power; marginal revenue; marginal cost; monopsony
notes: Pure competition, oligopoly and monopoly: their features, how competition among many sellers lowers costs and prices, how firms with market power use marginal analysis to set price and output, and competition on price and on other features. The skill: judge how much competition a real market has and what follows from it, with the grade 11 trusts as a historical case. Competition among buyers too: when one buyer dominates a market (a single large employer in a town), it can hold down the price it pays (monopsony). Open to grade 11 or 12 (Cory, 2026-11-13): this row does not require US History I. The example it once took from us1-industrialization is retaught here in brief, from the source, so a student who has not had that course is not lost.

words: productivity; human capital; physical capital; technology; wage; standard of living
notes: Why spending on research, equipment, technology and worker training raises productivity, and why higher productivity raises growth and living standards (the production possibilities curve moving out); how a worker's earnings depend on the market value of what they produce and on their productivity. Handoff kind: from wh2-postwar-prosperity (grade 10) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

standard: MA.ECON.T4.1; MA.ECON.T4.3; MA.ECON.T4.4; MA.ECON.T4.6; D2.Eco.6.9-12; D2.Eco.7.9-12
words: public good; market failure; externality; antitrust; natural monopoly; regulation; government failure
notes: Why government acts in markets: public goods and services, market failures and externalities, antitrust laws that promote competition (from the Sherman Act met in grade 11 to today), regulated natural monopolies such as utilities; and how policies can cost more than they return when goals other than efficiency drive them. The skill: weigh a policy's costs and benefits to judge whether it improved a market outcome. Open to grade 11 or 12 (Cory, 2026-11-13): this row does not require US History I. The example it once took from us1-progressivism is retaught here in brief, from the source, so a student who has not had that course is not lost.

words: revenue; progressive tax; proportional tax; regressive tax; deficit; surplus; national debt; marginal rate
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent of income)
notes: Government budgets: the main revenue and spending categories and their shares at the local, state and federal levels; progressive, proportional and regressive taxes; how changes in spending and taxes move deficits, surpluses and the debt; and (personal finance PFL.T1.3) how federal income tax rates on different incomes have changed since 1950, read from the rate tables. Builds on the 16th Amendment (1913) from grade 11. Builds on ss8-public-budget (grade 8); the handoff skips 3 grades because grades 9 to 11 are world and US history; government and economics are grade 12 courses. Handoff kind: from ss8-public-budget (grade 8) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss8-public-budget. Open to grade 11 or 12 (Cory, 2026-11-13): this row does not require US History I. The example it once took from us1-progressivism is retaught here in brief, from the source, so a student who has not had that course is not lost.

words: GDP; economic growth; unemployment rate; inflation; consumer price index; aggregate demand; aggregate supply
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent change)
notes: The circular flow diagram taught explicitly: households sell work to firms and buy their goods, firms pay wages and sell products, and government taxes and spends in both loops. How the whole economy is measured: GDP, growth, unemployment and inflation defined and how each is counted (and what each misses), aggregate supply and demand defined; causes of inflation and who gains and loses from it. Students use current indicators to describe the state of the economy and where it may be going. Aggregate supply and demand get their own graph, kept apart from the market graph. Handoff kind: from wh2-great-depression (grade 10) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: business cycle; expansion; recession; aggregate demand; aggregate supply; money supply; price level; real GDP
notes: National income, employment and prices as the result of household, business and government spending and production choices; aggregate supply and aggregate demand together setting unemployment and inflation; business cycles shaped by events in US history (the railroad booms and panics of grade 11, wars, new technologies). Students use current data to explain how changes in spending, production and the money supply affect the economy. The aggregate graph has different axes from the market graph: the price level against real GDP for the whole economy, not one good's price against its quantity. Open to grade 11 or 12 (Cory, 2026-11-13): this row does not require US History I. The example it once took from us1-market-revolution is retaught here in brief, from the source, so a student who has not had that course is not lost.

words: money; medium of exchange; store of value; unit of account; money supply; Federal Reserve
notes: What money does (medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account); what counts in the money supply; the roles of banks and other financial institutions; how the Federal Reserve System is organized and what it does, set against the fight over a national bank met in grade 11. Open to grade 11 or 12 (Cory, 2026-11-13): this row does not require US History I. The example it once took from us1-jackson-removal is retaught here in brief, from the source, so a student who has not had that course is not lost.

words: fiscal policy; monetary policy; interest rate; open market operations; stimulus; stabilization
notes: Fiscal and monetary policy defined; how taxing and spending decisions and the Federal Reserve's tools are used to pursue stable prices, full employment and growth; students evaluate which policy choices suit which conditions (a recession, high inflation), with cases from recent decades. Handoff kind: from wh2-great-depression (grade 10) (skips 1 grade because the courses between do not teach it) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

standard: MA.ECON.T7.1; MA.ECON.T7.2; MA.ECON.T7.3; MA.ECON.T7.4; MA.ECON.T7.8; D2.Eco.14.9-12
words: trade; specialization; absolute advantage; comparative advantage; tariff; quota; free trade
notes: Why individuals, regions and countries trade; absolute and comparative advantage worked from opportunity costs, and why most trade rests on comparative advantage; tariffs and quotas and why countries set them; the arguments for and against free trade weighed with evidence on who gains and who loses. Builds on wh2-globalization (grade 10); the handoff skips a grade because grade 11 US History I does not carry it; government and economics are grade 12 courses. Handoff kind: from wh2-globalization (grade 10) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: balance of trade; balance of payments; exchange rate; globalization; labor productivity
notes: The balance of trade and the balance of payments; US labor productivity compared with other developed countries; how exchange rate changes affect buying power at home and abroad; how globalization and competition for scarce resources affect growth, labor markets, rights, the environment and income in different nations, and lead to conflict or cooperation. Builds on wh2-globalization (grade 10); the handoff skips a grade because grade 11 US History I does not carry it; government and economics are grade 12 courses. Depth: grade 10 described who gained and lost from global trade; here students measure it with trade and income data. Handoff kind: from wh2-globalization (grade 10) is content revisited: this row reteaches it at its own depth and opens with a short retrieval task.

words: career; wage; salary; benefits; labor market; unemployment
notes: Personal finance: how people choose jobs they qualify for (satisfaction, pay, benefits, growth, location) and how the labor market sets wages; how a recession or a shift in an industry can cut income or end a job. Students sketch a first-year budget for one chosen job. Builds on ss8-public-budget (grade 8); the handoff skips 3 grades because grades 9 to 11 are world and US history; government and economics are grade 12 courses. Handoff kind: from ss8-public-budget (grade 8) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss8-public-budget.

words: advertising; influencer; payment method; rent-to-own; consumer protection; fee
notes: Personal finance: how advertising and social media move buying, read from studies of their effects; ways to pay (cash, debit and credit cards, checks, rent-to-own) and the true cost of each; the roles of state and federal governments in protecting consumers. Examples are made up, never real brands. New content: no earlier skill is assumed. The budget card from grades 3 to 8 opens with a short retrieval task. Economics' yearly action cycle: students choose one consumer question their peers face (a costly way to pay, a misleading offer), check it against public consumer-protection advice, and make a consumer information piece shared through the school. Action is the student's choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks.

words: principal; interest; compound interest; nominal rate; real rate; retirement account; deposit
cross_subject: math:F-LE.A.1c (growth by a constant percent)
notes: Personal finance: banks as businesses that lend depositors' money; principal, simple and compound interest (compound growth worked as growth by a constant percent); real and nominal interest rates; the credit, saving and investing services institutions offer; government policies that encourage saving (retirement and education accounts) and how well they work. Handoff kind: from ss8-public-budget (grade 8) (skips 3 grades because the courses between do not teach it) is dormant knowledge: the unit opens with a readiness check, and students who miss it get a one-lesson reteach of ss8-public-budget.

words: regulator; deposit insurance; Federal Reserve; Securities and Exchange Commission; consumer financial protection
notes: Personal finance: how well public agencies protect the banking system, markets and consumers (the Federal Reserve, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the FDIC, state banking departments, and the SEC's regulation of financial markets), judged with evidence from crises and enforcement records.

words: credit card; annual percentage rate; introductory rate; credit report; credit score; disclosure
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (interest as a percent)
notes: Personal finance: a card purchase is a loan, with fees and usually higher rates than other loans; why low introductory rates can jump after a late payment; credit bureaus, reports and scores, how they are used and what leads to denial; the right to full disclosure of loan terms and a free copy of one's own credit report. New content: no earlier skill is assumed. The budget card from grades 3 to 8 opens with a short retrieval task.

words: loan; down payment; term; repossession; garnishment; bankruptcy
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.B.4 (the loan payment formula from a geometric series)
notes: Personal finance: the long-term results of not repaying loans (damaged credit, repossession, wage garnishment, bankruptcy), then a credit plan for a major purchase such as a car or home that compares interest rates and terms and shows the total paid. Numbers are made-up offers, not real lenders. New content: no earlier skill is assumed. The budget card from grades 3 to 8 opens with a short retrieval task.

standard: MA.PFL.T3.7; MA.PFL.T3.8; MA.PFL.T3.9; MA.PFL.T2.6; MA.ECON.T2.11; MA.ECON.T6.6
words: asset; stock; bond; mutual fund; rate of return; diversification; risk
cross_subject: math:7.RP.A.3 (percent gain and loss)
notes: Personal finance and economics: financial markets move money from savers to investors; what a financial asset is and why its value rises and falls; how buyers and sellers set asset prices and so rates of return; why diversifying lowers risk; students track a made-up portfolio of stocks, bonds and funds on paper and write a savings or investment plan for a goal such as college or retirement. No real money and no individual company recommended.

words: insurance; premium; deductible; coverage; identity theft; scam
notes: Personal finance: the purposes of the main kinds of insurance (health, auto, renters or home, life, disability), then cost and coverage compared across several made-up quotes to pick the best fit for a described person; identity theft and how to protect personal information online, by email and by phone. New content: no earlier skill is assumed. The budget card from grades 3 to 8 opens with a short retrieval task.
